en: Preface:
Since the appearance of the six Buddhas in the world, it has been traditionally transmitted that they preached the Dharma to deliver sentient beings; yet, what they preached was not transmitted.

It was only upon reaching Śākyamuni Buddha that, during the assembly on Vulture Peak, he preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, finally declaring, "I have never spoken a single word. This is clearly visible.

It is said that there was originally nothing to be said. It was simply because he did not establish written words, transmitting a separate tradition outside the teachings, and entrusting it to Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"I transmit to you in secret the treasury of the true Dharma-eye; you must protect and uphold it.

He further commanded Ānanda to assist in the dual transmission and transformation, ensuring that it would never be severed. The bestowing of the verse and the robe began from this point. Thus it is in heaven.

In the land of Zhuguo (India), the lineage was transmitted successively through twenty-eight patriarchs. Fortunately, Bodhidharma, mindful of China and in accordance with the Buddha’s prophecy, projected his light there.

He then entrusted his disciple Upagupta (Bunuo Miltuoluo) to remain in India to propagate the Dharma, while he himself crossed the vast ocean, traveling for three full cycles of the seasons before finally reaching the South Sea. Finding no spiritual resonance with Emperor Wu of Liang, he remained [there].
At Shaolin, he encountered Shen Guang; truly, he had crossed oceans and deserts seeking the Dharma for the sake of others.

Though their meeting was not yet harmonized, those who appeared as if ignorant or dull-witted—Huike ultimately attained peace of mind and Sengcan purified his transgressions—without there being any divergent paths.

This is what is meant by the saying: "The ultimate Way is without difficulty; it is only the aversion to discernment that makes it so. The Fourth Patriarch waited patiently, and the Fifth Patriarch [repeatedly]...

The successive reception of the Dharma was in no way accidental. When it came to the Wayman Lu, while engaged in the lowly labor of gathering and selling firewood, he suddenly attained an understanding of the subtle principles of all Buddhas that transcended written words.
He regarded Xue Tong, who was renowned for his spiritual excellence both within and without the Buddhist teachings, as someone to be avoided by three li;
yet, the one who ultimately transmitted his Way was a man of the barbarian tribes from a cattle pen and slaughterhouse. From this point, the Southern and Northern Schools emerged.
The beginning: Those who succeeded the Sixth Patriarch were Nanyue and Qingyuan. From Nanyue came Mazu; from Mazu came Linji, Shigong, Yunmen, and Fayan.
Although there are four branches, Linji is considered the orthodox transmission. From Qingyuan came Shitou; from Shitou came Caodong.
Thus did the "one flower and five petals" begin here. Regarding the karmic conditions for the Dharma, it can be said that Linji was preeminent in its elucidation.
It is nearly exhausted. It is no more than inheriting the lineage of Shaoshi and seeking someone who is not deluded by others.
Xinghua realized the principle of Master Jie receiving a blow from Huangbo, yet his offering of incense had a specific master;
Fengxue’s questions and answers were entirely transformative, yet Shoushan’s place of realization was not at Fahua; Fenyang’s transformation occurred not where he set down his chopsticks.
All have their original faces and eyes intact from time immemorial. Ciming slowly adjusted his tattered robes;
he did not fail the Lion of Xihe. Yangqi knew such matters; Baiyun attained awakening upon meeting people. How true it is that "where others dwell, I do not dwell;
where others walk, I do not walk. Fushan guided Wuzu, who relied upon Baiyun. Why?
Ultimate impartiality and selflessness—if one is thus, the fruit of Buddhahood is realized from top to bottom. Cutting through the tangles of conceptual entanglement:
Xiangzuosheng of Huqiu shook the snoring of the assembly; Ying’an inherited the direct pulse of Yangqi; Miman called Fayan a "sand basin";
Wuzhun received the instructions of Po’an and did not seize the monkey; Gaofeng’s pillow and Sheng Zhongfeng.
The bamboo whisk: when this meaning is brought forth, everyone is liberated from verbal expression. Whether it be seeing the pine tree and suddenly awakening, or where the lamp-flower falls;

whether it be the fire singeing the eyebrows, or the water dripping onto the stalks of vegetables; or being without any exposed sharp edges—in all these cases, one cannot deceive him by even a single point.
As for those whose occupation is woodcutting, they may gain realization upon touching a stack of firewood; they are like the Sixth Patriarch.
They follow the same track. Yet, with his single white staff, Elder Mi revitalized the Linji school’s tradition; he was truly a peerless figure throughout the ages.
For Master Feiyin, it is even more difficult in these present times. It is not that he does not possess the far-reaching, open-mindedness of Master Huiyuan.
Daoyu Wang was a man of great integrity, yet the world’s practice of seizing and plundering remained as it was before;

it was not that he did not admire the noble conduct of Haizhou, who found his own teacher, nor that he did not honor Cunjang, who recognized and recommended his master, yet the world’s frantic competition for status remained as it was. This extends even to the matters of honoring one's ancestors and revering one's clan.
He received the lineage without conceit; a paragon of great filial piety and a supreme friend, he honored the natural bond between water and wood and cherished those of the same vital breath.

Yet, as the world remains steeped in its age-old corruption, he maintained a straightforward mind and upright conduct, acting with ultimate public-spiritedness and freedom from self-interest. The Elder Mi (Mimoluo) praised him, and others were likewise able to appreciate his worth.
Having resided at renowned monasteries throughout his career, he renovated halls and constructed new buildings to perpetuate the illustrious legacy of his predecessors and follow in their footsteps.
Listen to what follows. Formerly, Confucius said, "He who knows me and he who blames me are both found in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
Mencius declared that his own merit was not inferior to that of Yu. I say that the merit of Master Fei is no less than that of Confucius and Mencius.

Whether they are the same or different, in sum, they have obscured the Buddha-vehicle and lost sight of their spiritual lineage; thus, they have become increasingly fragmented and divergent. Now, I am urgently compiling this single volume of the direct transmission. Examine it closely...
To clarify this for you: who could have their head severed, yet the Dharma cannot be disparaged? Who could have their body transformed, yet the Way cannot be slighted?
Who has emptied themselves to yield to the worthy? Who has shared the teacher’s vessel through a spiritual accord? Who has had their minds seal one another? Who has inherited bowl from bowl?

I have set forth these ancient precedents as acupuncture and moxibustion for the ears of the common folk, and as a drum-roll from the very bowels of the Buddha, entitled *The Guiding Needle*. How would I dare—
I say: I do not rely on the accumulated virtues of venerable seniors, nor would I dare claim to have clarified the "Month-Day" (the assessment of character) for all eternity.
Yet, perhaps by using a single drop of lion’s milk to scatter ten bushels of donkey’s milk, there may be some small contribution.

I humbly pray that those who open this volume will witness the Way in their very sight, reflect upon the fact that it is inherent in every person and perfectly complete in each individual, and thus look back to the Seven Buddhas.

Why is it that the noble traces of the successive patriarchs flourished so uniquely in antiquity? Examining downward from the Sixth Patriarch to the Great Master of the thirty-fifth generation, why are their merits so abundant and magnificent?
It is evident that there is no duality between the Buddha and the monk; they do not inherit one another's legacy.
One need only resolutely block off deviant knowledge and deviant views, reflect inwardly, and turn the light back upon itself; then, one will penetrate through with clarity. As it is said:
White clouds obscure the traces of one’s former path; in the twelfth month, the fire burning the mountains is still bright red.

Once again, the breeze of compassion comes to fan it forth, so that where there was cold and ice, there is now warm and glowing heat. When the cover is opened, one sees light; when closed, one sees darkness.
Neither opening nor closing, it is majestically revealed. Past and future are not separated by even a single thread. Thus, one looks with the eyes and looks with the mind.
Thus one sees the heavy striking of ice within the fire. Alas! On a clear night, the moon shines upon the cold plum blossoms; on a frosty night, the frost strikes the sparse wooden leaves.
Relying on this Way, I urge my companions in the Dharma, gradually causing the pure wind to spread across the nine realms.

On the day of Ascending the Heights during the autumn of the Renchen year, Xu Changzhi visited his father Zhou and inscribed this preface for the *Catalogue of the Direct Lineage Guide to the Patriarchal Hall* within Daye Hall.
Volume One:
The Seven Buddhas—
Vipaśyin Buddha and Śikhin Buddha.
Vipaśyin Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha,
Kanakamuni Buddha, Kāśyapa Buddha,
and Śākyamuni Buddha.
The Patriarchs of the Western Heaven:
First Patriarch, Venerable Mahākāśyapa; Second Patriarch, Venerable Ānanda;
Third Patriarch, Venerable Śaṇakavāsin; Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta.
The Fifth Patriarch, Venerable Diṭṭhika; the Sixth Patriarch, Venerable Miṅgaka;
the Seventh Patriarch, Venerable Vasumitra; the Eighth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhanandi;
the Ninth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhamitra; and the Tenth Patriarch, Venerable Pārśva.
The Venerable Eleventh Patriarch Punanayasa; the Venerable Twelfth Patriarch Aśvaghoṣa Bodhisattva;
the Venerable Thirteenth Patriarch Kambalāmbara; the Venerable Fourteenth Patriarch Nāgārjuna;
the Venerable Fifteenth Patriarch Kanadeva; and the Venerable Sixteenth Patriarch Rāhulata.
The Seventeenth Patriarch, Venerable Saṃghanandin; the Eighteenth Patriarch, Venerable Gayāsata;
the Nineteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kumārajīva; the Twentieth Patriarch, Venerable Śamadatta;
and the Twenty-first Patriarch, Venerable Vasupujya.
The Twenty-second Patriarch, Venerable Maṇḍara; the Twenty-third Patriarch, Venerable Huike (Haklenā);
the Twenty-fourth Patriarch, Venerable Śiṣyabhikṣu (Sizi);
the Twenty-fifth Patriarch, Venerable Vasubandhu (Poshasidu).
The twenty-sixth patriarch was Venerable Ratnamitra;
the twenty-seventh patriarch was Venerable Prajñātāra;
the twenty-eighth patriarch was Venerable Bodhidharma.

The Patriarchs of the Eastern Land (beginning with Bodhidharma’s arrival from the West; after six generations came Caoxi. Following Caoxi, the lineage split into two branches. One was Nanyue Huairang.)

From Mazu Daoyi emerged one: Baizhang Huaihai. From Huaihai, Tianwang awakened; from Huaihai emerged Shanzhao of Mount Gui (Guishan Lingyou) and Huairang of Huangbo (Huangbo Xiyun). From Lingyou emerged Dayi of Yangshan (Yangshan Huiji); this is the Guiyang school. From Xiyun emerged Linji Yixuan; this is the Linji school.

From the realization of Longtan Xuanzang, the lineage was transmitted successively to Yunmen Wenyan; this is the Yunmen school. Fayan Wenyi is the founder of the Fayan school. As for the other, Qingyuan Xingsi: from Si it was transmitted to Shitou Xiqian and Tianhuang Daowu.
The realization was severed. [The lineage] was transmitted in succession to Dongshan Liangjie; Liangjie transmitted it to Yunju Daoying.
This is the Cao-Dong school. First Patriarch: Master Bodhidharma Second Patriarch: Master Huike Third Patriarch:
Mahāsattva Sengcan Fourth Patriarch: Master Daoxin
The Great Master Hongren, the Fifth Patriarch; The Great Master Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch, Scroll One;

The Third Generation: Chan Master Baizhang Hai; The Fourth Generation: Chan Master Huangbo Yun; The Fifth Generation:

Chan Master Ying’an Huo; The Eighteenth Generation: Chan Master Mian Xianjie; The Nineteenth Generation:
