*The Direct Lineage Guide to the Patriarchal Garden*, Volume One.
Compiled and narrated by the Layman Wuyuan, Xu Changzhi Jinzhou.
The Seven Buddhas:
Vipaśyin Buddha (the 998th of the past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*). The verse says: "His body was born from within the signless; it is like..."

Like illusions that manifest various forms, the mental consciousness of the illusionist is fundamentally non-existent; both sin and merit are empty and have no place of abiding. (When the human lifespan was eighty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world.

He was of the Kṣatriya caste, his clan name was Kauṛiya, his father was Bandhu, and his mother was Bandhumatī. He resided in the city of Bandhumatī and sat beneath a Pāpala tree. He preached the Dharma in three assemblies, delivering three hundred and forty-eight thousand people.
He had two disciples with supernormal powers: the first was named Khaṇḍa, and the second was named Tissa.)
Śikhin Buddha (the ninth hundred and ninety-ninth Tathāgata of the *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*) spoke in verse: "All wholesome dharmas that arise are fundamentally illusory;
The commission of all evil karmas is likewise illusory. The body is like a mass of foam, the mind is like the wind; Illusory manifestations have no root and possess no real nature.

When the human lifespan was seventy thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was born into the Kṣatriya caste, of the Kauṛilya clan. His father was named Jyotiṣprabha and his mother was named Prabhāvatī. He resided in the city of Prabhāsa. He sat beneath a Puṇḍarīka tree and taught the Dharma in three assemblies, delivering two hundred and fifty thousand people. He possessed two disciples of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*).
First, Abhibhū; second, Viśvabhū Buddha (one thousand honored ones of the *Ratna-vyūha* Kalpa). A verse says:
"Taking the four great elements as a borrowed body, The mind is fundamentally unborn, arising only due to objects.
If the external object is absent, the mind is likewise non-existent; Sin and merit are like illusions—they arise and then perish. [This occurred] when the human lifespan was sixty thousand years.

This Buddha appeared in the world as a member of the Kṣatriya caste, with the clan name Koliya. His father was Sudīpa and his mother was named Śīlā. He resided in the city of Anupama and sat beneath a *piyāla* tree. He held two assemblies for preaching the Dharma and delivered one hundred and thirty thousand people across. He possessed two supernormal powers: first, he traveled through the air.

2. Krakucchanda Buddha (the first honored one of the Bhadrakalpa) spoke in verse: "To see that the body has no reality is the Buddha-body; To realize that the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha-illusion.
When one realizes that the nature of both body and mind is empty, How can such a person differ from the Buddha? [This occurred] when the human lifespan was forty thousand years.

This Buddha appeared in the world as a member of the Brahmin caste, with the clan name Kāśyapa. His father was named Riddha and his mother Sujātā; he resided in the city of Āndhavana. Sitting beneath a Śirīṣa tree, he delivered a single discourse on the Dharma, through which he liberated forty thousand people. He possessed two disciples of supernatural power: first, Sanni, and second, Vīra.

The Buddha Kanakamuni (the second of the two honored ones of the Bhadrakalpa) spoke in verse: "The Buddha does not perceive a body to know he is the Buddha; If there were truly a knowing subject, there would be no Buddha apart from it.

The wise are able to know that the nature of offenses is empty; They remain serene and unafraid of birth and death. [When the human lifespan was thirty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world.

He was of the Brahmin caste, of the Kāśyapa clan. His father was Mahāgaura and his mother was Sujaya. He resided in the city of Śuddhavatī and sat beneath an Udumbara tree. In a single assembly, he preached the Dharma and delivered thirty thousand people; he possessed the two supernormal powers.]
1. Śūpanna; 2. Uttara. (Kāśyapa Buddha [Third Honored One of the Bhadrakalpa]).
A verse says: "The nature of all sentient beings is pure; from the beginning, they are unborn and cannot be extinguished.

This very body and mind are born of illusion; within this illusory transformation, there is neither sin nor merit. (When the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world.)

He was of the Brahmin caste, of the Kāśyapa clan; his father was Brahmadeva and his mother was Vasudattā. He resided in the city of Vārāṇasī and sat beneath a Nyagrodha tree. At one assembly, he preached the Dharma and delivered twenty thousand people. His two disciples with supernormal powers were Tiṣya and Bhāradvāja.
Śākyamuni Buddha (the fourth honored one of the Bhadrakalpa) was of the Kṣatriya caste. His father was King Śuddhodana, and his mother was Māyā of the Kṣatriya clan.
Since the renewal of heaven and earth and the initial opening of Jambudvīpa, his family has served as kings for generations.

Having practiced the path through successive kalpas, he received a prophecy from Dīpaṃkara Buddha that he would become a Buddha in this kalpa. Subsequently, during the era of Kāśyapa Buddha, by means of bodhi-...
Śākyamuni attained the Way and ascended to be born in the Tuṣita Heaven, where he was named the Great Being Vajragarbha (Huming Dashi).

When the time for his manifestation arrived, he descended his spirit into Māyā. This occurred in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhou Zhao’s reign, on the eighth day of the fourth month of the Jiayin year.
He was born from the right side of Māyā; at the moment of birth, he emitted the radiance of great wisdom, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.
From the realm, golden lotus flowers sprang from the earth, spontaneously supporting his two feet.

With one hand pointing to heaven and the other pointing to the earth, he walked seven paces and looked toward the four quarters, saying: "In all the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am honored. (As soon as he emerged from the womb, his entire being was manifest;

pointing to heaven and pointing to earth, he proclaimed himself to humanity. He led countless deluded men and women, leaving nothing hidden between heaven and man. Yunmen said: "Had I seen him at that time, I would have struck him dead with a single blow and fed him to the dogs, so as to ensure peace throughout the world.")
From the time of his birth, various miraculous wonders occurred, as fully described in the sūtras.
When he reached the age of nineteen, in the eighth day of the second month of the forty-second year, desiring to seek renunciation, he thought to himself, "What further encounter shall I have?

He then went out for an excursion through the four gates and beheld the four conditions of birth, old age, sickness, and death. His heart was moved by both sorrow and joy, and he reflected upon them. This...

"Aging, illness, and death—these must ultimately be renounced. Then, at the hour of midnight, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens appeared within the window, joined his palms, and said, "The time for your renunciation has arrived;
you may depart. Thereupon, the devas supported the hooves of the horse he rode, and he soared through the air, leaping over the city walls and departing.
He vowed: "Until I sever the eightfold suffering and realize unexcelled Bodhi, I shall not return."

Without turning the Wheel of Dharma, he would never return. King Śuddhodana pondered this deeply and dispatched tens of thousands of his ministers to persuade him to return to the palace, but he remained resolute and did not turn back.
He entered Mount Taṇḍula to practice the Way, beginning at the abode of Ārāḍa Kālāma.
For three years he studied under Ārāḍa Kālāma, but when he realized that the state of meditative concentration was not the ultimate goal, he abandoned it.
He then went to Udraka Rāmaputra and for three years studied the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; realizing this too was not the final truth, he likewise abandoned it.

He then went to Mount Vulture Peak and joined the various non-Buddhist ascetics, subsisting on only sesame and wheat for six years. The World-Honored One reflected to himself: "This asceticism is not the true liberation. I...
Only after receiving food would he attain Buddhahood. He then bathed in the Nairañjanā River; the gods bent down a tree for him, and the World-Honored One reached out and emerged.
He accepted the milk-gruel offered by the daughter of the cowherd, and immediately proceeded to the foot of the Pippala tree.

The Heavenly Emperor manifested a person who gathered auspicious grass for the World-Honored One to sit upon. Auspicious clouds and propitious winds arose from all four directions, swirling and spreading.

When the celestial Māras perceived that the World-Honored One had attained the Way and would soon be subject to their defeat, they led their hosts to create obstacles, manifesting every conceivable scene of terror and desire.
Yet the World-Honored One remained unmoved; he pressed the earth with his finger, and the great earth shook violently, causing the Māras to fall prostrate. Thereupon—
He subdued them. Thus, the Sūtra says: "With no mind, no intention, and no conditioned activity, he utterly overcomes all non-Buddhists.
Having first tested them with heterodox methods, he demonstrated various skillful means and aroused their diverse views, leading them to Bodhi.

Then, on the evening of the seventh day of the second month in the third year of King Mu’s reign, the *guīwèi* year, he entered the Samādhi of Rightness. On the eighth day, when the morning star appeared, [he passed away].
At that time, he attained great enlightenment and realized perfect awakening. He then sighed, saying: "How marvelous! All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata;
yet, because of delusive thoughts and attachments, they are unable to realize it. At that time, he was thirty years of age.
Six years after his attainment of the Way, he returned to preach the Dharma for King Śuddhodana. The King was greatly delighted and dispatched five members of his clan.
The Hundred Noble Sons followed him into the homeless life. One day, the World-Honored One ascended the seat, and when the great assembly had gathered and settled, Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said:
"Observe clearly the Dharma of the Dharma-King; the Dharma of the Dharma-King is thus. Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from the seat.

(Only those among the sages who have realized the essence would know that the Dharma of the Dharma-King does not proceed in this manner. If there were a *siddhārtha* guest within the assembly, why would Mañjuśrī need to strike the gavel once? [This should have been resolved] precisely before he had even ascended the seat. The World-Honored One—
The sun rose and [the Buddha] took his seat. He sat in silence. Ānanda struck the gavel and said, "I request the World-Honored One to preach the Dharma.
The World-Honored One said, "In this assembly there is a bhikṣu who has committed an offense against the Vinaya; therefore, I shall not preach the Dharma.
Using his power of reading others' minds, Ānanda observed the bhikṣu and subsequently had him expelled. The World-Honored One remained silent once more. Ānanda spoke again: "Just now, because of..."
Two bhikṣus had violated the Vinaya. Having expelled these two bhikṣus, the World-Honored One did not preach the Dharma.

The World-Honored One said, "I vow never to preach the Dharma for those of the Two Vehicles, such as the śrāvakas. He then descended from his seat. (The first arrow was light, but the second arrow was deep;

out of compassion, the World-Honored One showed this to Ānanda. How many people here will give rise to profound reflection? One day, the World-Honored One ascended the seat. Kāśyapa struck the gavel and said, "World-Honored One..."
Having finished preaching the Dharma, he descended from his seat (thus ascending the seat, thus striking the gavel, thus preaching the Dharma, thus descending from the seat—thus, thus).
While the World-Honored One was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven preaching the Dharma for his mother, King Udayana missed the Buddha and commanded a craftsman to carve a sandalwood image.

When the World-Honored One descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the image also came out to welcome him. The World-Honored One called out three times and the image responded three times; thereupon [the Buddha] said: "The Unconditioned is True."

"The Buddha is truly within my body. When the World-Honored One was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for ninety days and was about to take leave of the celestial realm to descend, the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings all went to the void to welcome him.
There was a bhikṣuṇī named Padmavarṇā who thought to herself:
"I am a bhikṣuṇī; I must necessarily wait behind the great saṃgha of monks to see the Buddha.

It would be better for me to use my supernatural power to transform myself into a Cakravartin King, surrounded by a thousand sons, so that I may be the very first to see the Buddha and thus fulfill my vow. As soon as the World-Honored One saw her, he rebuked her, saying:
"Utpalavarṇā Bhikṣuṇī, how can you bypass the great saṃgha of monks to see me? Although you see my physical body (rūpakāya),..."
Furthermore, Subhūti, while you do not see my Dharma-body when sitting in meditation within a cave, you nevertheless see my Dharma-body (after all, which body is it?).
The World-Honored One showed a mani-jewel that changes according to color and asked the Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions, "What color is this jewel?
At that time, the Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions each spoke of it as having a different color. The World-Honored One concealed the jewel and again raised his hand, saying, "This jewel..."
"What color is it? The Heavenly King said, "The Buddha’s hand has no pearls; where could there be any color? The World-Honored One said, "How can you be so utterly deluded?
When I show you a worldly pearl, you insist on saying it has blue, yellow, red, or white colors.
When I show you a true pearl, you know nothing at all. At that time, the Heavenly Kings of the five directions all attained realization of the Way themselves. (Worldly pearls; true pearls.)
From what basis is this distinction made? When the Brahmin Kāla offered a *saṃyukta* flower from the *udumbara* tree, the World-Honored One called to the ṛṣi, saying, "Put it down.
The Brahmin put down the flower in his left hand. The Buddha again called to the ṛṣi, saying, "Put it down."
The Brahmin then let go of a flower from his right hand. The Buddha again called out to the immortal, "Let it go!
The Brahmin said, "Now both my hands are empty; what more do you command me to let go of? The Buddha replied, "I am not instructing you to discard those flowers.
You should let go of the six external objects (*ṣaḍ-bāhyaviṣaya*), the six internal faculties (*ṣaḍ-ādhyātmikendriya*), and the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) all at once."

"However, there is no place where anything can be abandoned. This is the place where you lay down your body and life. At these words, the Brahmin realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

(Since one has already abandoned the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses, what place is there that cannot be abandoned? This is the place of liberation from birth and death. Furthermore, what is called the "patience of non-arising"?

The World-Honored One, because the Bodhisattva Universal Eye wished to see Samantabhadra but could not find him, entered into meditative concentration three times in succession and surveyed the three [realms].
Throughout a thousand great trichiliocosms, he searched for Samantabhadra but could not find or see him. He then came before the Buddha and said, "The Buddha said:
'You need only give rise to a single thought within the samādhi of stillness, and you will immediately see Samantabhadra. Thereupon, as soon as Wubian gave rise to that single thought,"

Then he saw Samantabhadra heading toward the sky, riding a six-tusked white elephant. (Cloud Abode Dao says: "Puyan toppled the World-Honored One; the World-Honored One toppled Puyan. Tell me, where is Puyan?

He cannot avoid being laughed at by the bystanders. Alas! Who is the bystander? Because of this, when a seer with five supernatural powers asked the World-Honored One, "The World-Honored One possesses six powers;
I possess five. What is that one power? the Buddha called out to the seer with five powers. The seer—

The man assented. The Buddha said: "Which one penetration? You ask me [about] the five penetrations, the six penetrations, or hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of penetrations, yet none of them transcend that one penetration."
One day the World-Honored One commanded Ānanda: "The time for the meal is approaching; you should enter the city with your alms bowl.
Ānanda assented. The World-Honored One said: "Since you are carrying the bowl, you must follow the ritual protocol of the seven Buddhas of the past. Ānanda then asked:
"What is the ritual of the Seven Buddhas? The World-Honored One called to Ānanda, and Ānanda responded. The World-Honored One said, "Take this bowl and go.

(The essential countenance of Buddha after Buddha must appear before one; Gautama preached the "old woman’s Chan" for him. Alas, Ānanda departed in shame, still waiting for someone to pull down the bannerpole.

When the World-Honored One was on the path to enlightenment, he spread his hair to cover the mud and offered flowers to Dīpaṃkara Buddha. Seeing the place where the hair had been spread, Dīpaṃkara then signaled for the assembly to withdraw.
He then pointed to the ground and said, "On this plot of land, a Brahma-shrine (Brahma-vihāra) should be established.

At that time, there was among the assembly a wise elder who took a banner and, inserting it at the spot indicated by the finger, declared, "The construction of the Brahma-shrine is complete. Thereupon, the various devas scattered flowers and offered their praise.
Once, while the World-Honored One was walking with Ānanda, he saw an ancient stūpa of a Buddha.
The World-Honored One then paid his respects. Ānanda asked, "Whose stūpa is this? The World-Honored One replied, "It is the stūpa of the Buddhas of the past.
Ānanda asked, "Of whom were the Buddhas of the past disciples? The World-Honored One replied, "They were my disciples. Ānanda said, "That must be so..."
"It shall be so. On the day of the *pravāraṇā*, Mañjuśrī had spent the summer retreats in three places.
When Kāśyapa was about to strike the gavel to expel him, as soon as he raised the gavel, he saw hundreds of thousands of millions of Mañjuśrīs. Kāśyapa exhausted all his supernatural powers.
The mallet could not be lifted. The World-Honored One then asked Kāśyapa, "Whom do you intend to expel, Mañjuśrī? Kāśyapa had no reply.

(Kāśyapa’s supernatural powers were indeed such that he should have first seized the Yellow-Faced Old Man and expelled him. To the east of the city there was an old woman who was born at the same time as the Buddha;

she did not wish to see the Buddha. Every time she saw the Buddha approaching, she would immediately avoid him. Nevertheless, whenever she looked back toward the east or west, [she saw him everywhere].
"All are Buddhas. Thereupon, he covered his face with his hand; even within the palms of his ten fingers, they were all entirely Buddhas. (The old woman did not wish to see the Buddha;

when the wind subsided and the waves became calm, east and west were entirely Buddhas. "When the water rises, the boat is high. Because Mañjuśrī arrived at the place where the Buddhas had gathered, he found that the various Buddhas had each returned to their own abodes.
Only one woman remained sitting near the Buddha, having entered into *samādhi*. Mañjuśrī...
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying, "How is it that this person is able to approach the Buddha while I am not?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "You need only awaken this woman and cause her to rise from samādhi; you may ask her yourself. Mañjuśrī circumambulated the woman three times.
He snapped his fingers once, and then, exerting all his supernatural powers, he tried to lift her up to the Brahma Heaven; yet he was unable to bring her out.
The World-Honored One said, "Even if there were hundreds of thousands of Mañjuśrīs, they too would be unable to bring this woman out of her samādhi.
Forty-two *gaṅgā*-sands of lands below here, there is the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti (Wǎngmíng), who can bring this woman out of her samādhi. Immediately, Vimalakīrti...
The Great Being emerged from the earth and paid homage to the World-Honored One.

The World-Honored One commanded Wuming to go forth; Wuming then went before the woman and snapped his fingers once. Thereupon, the woman emerged from her meditative absorption. (Setting aside for now the question of whether she "emerged" or "did not emerge"—how is this absorption to be understood?

In short, one must see through the pivotal mechanism within it; there is not a single dharma that differs from the ordinary. The Buddha-nature is the matter of original truth; who says there is another teacher? At the place where Wuming snapped his fingers, the woman emerged from *dhyāna*. It costs nothing.)

Not even a hair’s breadth of force has ever moved what the mind conceives. All sentient beings are fundamentally equal; it is only in daily life that one harbors many doubts. Aṅgulimāla once went to the gate of a wealthy man’s house carrying his alms bowl.
At that moment, the man’s wife was in the throes of a difficult childbirth. The man said, "Disciple of Gautama, you are a most holy being.
What dharma do you possess that can free her from this suffering of childbirth? Aṅgulimāla replied to the man, "I have only recently entered the Way and have not yet—"
"Know this dharma. Wait for me to return and ask the World-Honored One; I shall come back and inform you. Upon his return, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Aṅgulimāla, "Go quickly and tell her: 'Since I followed the Dharma of the Noble Ones, I have never killed a living being.

Aṅgulimāla received the Buddha’s words and went swiftly to inform her. When his wife heard this, she gave birth at that very moment. (The Buddha does not kill; when a woman gives birth, the sun rises.)

Dongshan. The moon sinks behind the western ridge. Before Mount Huayin lies a hundred-foot well; within it, cold spring water pierces the bones. Whose beautiful lady comes to view her reflection? She does not look at anything else, but gazes at the side of her neck.
One day, when Mañjuśrī was standing outside the gate, the World-Honored One said, "Mañjuśrī, Mañjuśrī, why do you not enter the gate?
Mañjuśrī replied, "I do not see a single dharma outside the gate. Why do you instruct me to enter? (Outside the gate, entering the gate.)
Set that aside for now. What do you call a "gate"? Bodhisattva Anantagātra took a bamboo staff to measure the crown of the World-Honored One’s head;
it measured one *zhang* and six *chi*, then another *zhang* and six *chi*. He continued measuring up to the Brahma Heaven, yet he could not see the top of the Buddha’s head.

Thereupon, he cast down the bamboo staff, joined his palms, and spoke this verse: "Space has no boundaries, And the Buddha’s merits are likewise. Were there anyone able to measure them, Even through the exhaustion of kalpas..."

[This was] "exhausting [the limit]" (the Bodhisattva Anantagātra failed to measure himself, yet measured the World-Honored One’s inexhaustible crown; he could not avoid this one additional case of doubt).
At that time, because the Gandharva King presented music, the mountains, rivers, and great earth all produced the sound of lutes. Kāśyapa rose and performed a dance. The King asked:
“Kāśyapa, are you not an arhat whose outflows are exhausted? How can there still be residual habits? The Buddha said, “In truth, there are no residual habits;
do not slander the Dharma. The king then played the lute three times, and Kāśyapa likewise danced three times.
The King said, "Kāśyapa performed a dance; was that not practicing? The Buddha said, "In truth, he never performed a dance.

The King said, "World-Honored One, how can you speak falsely? The Buddha said, "It is no falsehood. When you plucked the lute, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the wood, and the stone all produced the sound of the lute;
was that not so? The King said, "It was. The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa was exactly like this; therefore, it is true."

He never performed a dance. Thus the King believed and accepted [the teaching that] "the sound of the wind and the resonance of the water are nothing other than music; every dharma is fully manifest as the original perfection.

While the World-Honored One was in the Sixth Heaven, preaching the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, he commanded all fierce and malevolent ghosts and spirits from other lands, this land, the human realm, and the heavens to assemble together.
They were to receive the Buddha’s entrustment and protect the True Dharma. He decreed that if there were any who did not attend, the Four Heavenly Kings...
The Gate-Kings flew hot iron wheels after them, compelling them to assemble. Once they had gathered, there was not one who did not comply with the Buddha’s command;
each made a great vow to protect the True Dharma. Only one Māra King remained, who said to the World-Honored One: "Gautama!"
"I shall wait until all sentient beings have attained Buddhahood and the realm of sentient beings is emptied, such that even the name 'sentient being' no longer exists;

only then will I resolve to attain Bodhicitta" (O King of Maras, King of Maras! Identify that which constitutes Bodhicitta. Even if all sentient beings were to attain Buddhahood and the realm of sentient beings were emptied, leaving no name for "sentient beings," would it still be permitted to resolve upon the mind?).
World-Honored One, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, five hundred bhikṣus attained the four dhyānas.
They possessed the five supernormal powers but had not yet attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).

By means of their supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), they each saw for themselves how they had killed their fathers and harmed their mothers, as well as other grave offenses. Within their own minds, they each harbored doubts and were unable to realize or enter the profound Dharma.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, took a sharp sword in his hand and held it toward the Tathāgata, O World-Honored One.
He then said to Mañjuśrī, "From the very beginning, there has been no self or person; it is only because of the internal mind that one perceives a self or person.
When the internal mind arises, the 'self' is inevitably harmed; this is precisely what is called 'harm. Thereupon, the five hundred bhikṣus—"
He realized for himself that his original mind is like a dream and like an illusion; within this dream and illusion, there is no self, no person, and not even the parents who gave birth to him.
Thereupon, the five hundred bhikṣus praised him in unison, saying: "Mañjuśrī, the Great Sage of Wisdom, has profoundly penetrated the very source of the Dharma.
Though he held a sharp sword in his hand and pressed it against the body of the Tathāgata, the sword was as the Buddha was—both were one."
Marks are non-dual; the markless is unproduced. Within this, how could there be killing? (Mañjuśrī, for the sake of another’s private affair, he prolonged his ignorance;

he brought misfortune upon five hundred bhikṣus, beating them until they lost their nostrils. Nevertheless, do you still recognize where the World-Honored One has fallen? The World-Honored One, because King Prasenajit asked: "Within ultimate truth, is there conventional truth?
If one says there is not, then wisdom should not be dual. If one says there is, then wisdom should not be single."
"As for the meaning of 'one' and 'two,' what is that meaning? The Buddha said, "Great King, in the past, during the time of Dragon Light Buddha (Nāgaprabhāsa), you once asked about this very meaning.
Now I say nothing, and you hear nothing. This state of neither speaking nor hearing is the meaning of 'one' and 'two.

(The World-Honored One spoke until his mouth was full; the King of Kośala listened until his ears were full. Where, then, is the place of neither speaking nor hearing? Try to examine this closely. The World-Honored One [spoke thus] because of the Brahmin Dīrghanakha.
Hui-ssu challenged [Vasubandhu] to a debate on doctrine, making a solemn agreement: "If my thesis falls into error, I shall decapitate myself as an apology.
The World-Honored One asked, "What is the fundamental tenet of your thesis? Hui-ssu replied, "My tenet is that I accept nothing at all.

The World-Honored One asked, "Do you accept this view or not? Hui-ssu flung his sleeves and departed. While traveling halfway home, he attained realization and sighed, saying, "My thesis has two flaws."
"I am defeated. If this view is accepted, my position is defeated at a coarse level; if this view is not accepted, my position is defeated at a subtle level.
No humans, devas, or followers of the two vehicles understand where my doctrine falls into defeat; only the World-Honored One and the great Bodhisattvas know where my doctrine falls into defeat.
Returning before the World-Honored One, he said, "My doctrine is defeated on both counts. Therefore, I shall behead myself as an apology."
The World-Honored One said, "In my Dharma, there is no such matter. You should turn your mind toward the Way.

Thereupon, together with his five hundred followers, he simultaneously threw himself before the Buddha, left the household life, and realized arhatship. (If one holds this view and accepts it, one destroys one's family; if one holds this view and does not accept it, with whom can one debate?)

The carrying pole suddenly breaks and both ends fall off; within a single hair-tip, heaven and earth appear. The wheel of the Dharma has never yet turned; were it to turn, it would surely run toward both extremes. When the bright mirror suddenly confronts the stand, beauty and ugliness are distinguished in that very moment. As beauty and ugliness are distinguished, the clouds of compassion open.

Where can dust arise at the Gate of Compassion? Thinking of the fine horse that glimpsed the shadow of the whip, it chases the wind for a thousand *li*—can it be called back? This seeing and receiving, or not? One turns further into confusion; suddenly realizing one’s error, one discerns one’s own person.

After the wind and rain have passed over the peach blossoms by the roadside, where can a horse’s hoof avoid the remaining petals? When the World-Honored One was at the assembly on Vulture Peak, he held up a flower to show the multitude.
At that time, the entire assembly remained silent, except for the Venerable Kāśyapa, who broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said: "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye."
The wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*, the true mark which is markless, this subtle and profound Dharma-gate does not rely on words or letters;

it is a separate transmission outside the teachings, entrusted to Mahākāśyapa. (In the bustling marketplace, the tile struck the brick; the culprit was surely hit. Had he overturned the meditation seat at that moment, later descendants would not have claimed there was a "real dharma" transmitted.
When the World-Honored One reached the Many-Sons Stūpa, he commanded Mahākāśyapa to share his seat and sit, and with the Saṃgha...

He surrounded him with the *kāṣāya* robe and then entrusted to him the protection and maintenance of the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma (*saddharmakṣayanidhi*), commanding Ānanda to act as his deputy in propagating the teachings so that they would not be severed.
He then spoke this verse: "The Dharma is originally without dharma; The dharma-less dharma is also dharma.
Now, at the time of entrusting the dharma-less, How has any dharma ever been a dharma? At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, he again addressed Kā...
"Kāśyapa, I shall entrust this golden-threaded saṃghāṭī robe to you. Transmit it to the one who is to succeed me, so that it shall not decay until the appearance of the Buddha Maitreya.
When Kāśyapa heard these verses, he prostrated with his head at [the Buddha's] feet and said, "Excellent, excellent!"

"I shall comply with your command, out of reverent obedience to the Buddha. (This concludes the account of the flower and the smile; it is not known how this established the patriarchal style. If one says that mind and eye are simultaneously realized, one cannot avoid remaining in a state of dimness within a dream.
When the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvana, the Great Being Mañjuśrī requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma once more.
The World-Honored One rebuked him, saying: "Mañjuśrī, during my forty-nine years in the world, I have never spoken a single word. You request me..."

"Turning the Wheel of Dharma again—is this not the Wheel of Dharma I have previously turned? (The Yellow-Faced Gautama, while in the kingdom of Magadha at the Bodhimanda of the Aranya-dharma, within a single mote of dust shattered that very mote of dust and expounded the vast realm of the Tathāgata;
his wondrous voice resonated afar, reaching everywhere, and he said: 'In my forty-nine years of dwelling in the world, I have never spoken a single word.'")"
At the assembly for the Parinirvāṇa, the World-Honored One stroked his chest with his hand and addressed the multitude, saying:
"You should all carefully contemplate my body, which is the color of purple-polished gold. Behold it fully and take satisfaction in it; do not let yourselves have cause for regret later.

If you say that I have entered extinction, you are not my disciples; if you say that I have not entered extinction, you likewise are not my disciples. At that time, a multitude of hundreds of billions all attained [realization].

"Awakening to the truth: 'The eternal abode of a thousand years rests upon a single morning's monk; look at others—what are they doing? At that time, the World-Honored One arrived at the city of Kuśinagara and addressed the great assembly:

'I now suffer from back pain and wish to enter nirvana. He then proceeded to the side of the Hiranyavati River, beneath a pair of śāla trees, and lay down on his right side with his feet叠疊 (one foot upon the other), entering a state of profound stillness and tranquility.
Furthermore, he rose from his coffin to preach the Dharma for his mother, specifically manifesting the pair."
[The Buddha] was satisfied. He converted Vakkali and spoke the verse on impermanence: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing.
With the cessation of arising and ceasing, nirvāṇa is bliss. At that time, the disciples immediately vied with one another to cremate him with fragrant wood. After the embers were extinguished...
The golden coffin remained as it was. At that time, the great assembly, standing before the Buddha, praised him with these verses:
"How can the fierce and blazing fires of the common world Bring about the cremation of this golden body? We pray that the Honored One’s fire of samādhi May perform the cremation of this golden form.

Thereupon, the golden coffin rose from its seat to a height of seven *tāla* trees. Moving back and forth through the air, it manifested the fire of samādhi, and in an instant, [the body] became ashes.
He was born. Eight *hu* and four *dou* of *śarīra* were obtained. This was the year Ren-shen, the fifty-second year of King Mu.

On the fifteenth day of the second month, [the Buddha entered nirvana] before even leaving the royal palace; why then would his two feet need to be exposed from the golden coffin, causing Kāśyapa’s eyebrows to knit in distress? While Ānanda stood before the gate, the *yaṣṭi* (banner-pole) fell; as he was about to depart, he stretched out his two legs.
(Tread upon the pit of [tasting] cessation).
The First Patriarch of the Western Heaven, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, was a native of Magadha. His clan name was Brahmin; his father was named Yin... (drinking).
Zé’s mother was named Xiāngzhì. In a past life, she was a goldsmith. She encountered the parinirvāṇa of Vipaśyin Buddha, when the fourfold assembly erected a stūpa for him.
A poor woman obtained a gold bead and earnestly requested the goldsmith to repair a missing portion of the golden face on the Buddha image within the stūpa.
Together they made a vow that they would be husband and wife without a formal marriage in every successive lifetime. Due to these causes and conditions, [they were so for] ninety-one...
For kalpas, their bodies were entirely golden. They were again husband and wife with this woman, the Golden Light Nī;
her name in the Sanskrit language is Kāśyapa, which here means "Drinker of Light," a name derived from the radiance of her body. Yet both husband and wife dwelt in purity, free from worldly thoughts.
They soon thereafter left the household life and practiced the dhūta austerities. Then, a deity in the sky addressed them, saying: "The Buddha has already..."
He left the world and requested to go and study under him. The Venerable One immediately hurried to pay homage to the World-Honored One at the Bamboo Grove Monastery.
The Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu. His beard and hair fell away of their own accord. Among the assembly, the Buddha praised him as the foremost.

Later, due to the occasion of the plucking of the flower (a single flower was just plucked; the hearts of a thousand sages trembled. Meeting an ignorant fellow, he smiled and acted; like fire on dead wood, it shines brilliantly through all time), the Dharma was entrusted to him at the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
The Venerable One was at the Pipphaliguhā Cave. With his purified divine eye, he saw that the World-Honored One had entered parinirvāṇa on the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī River.
He immediately went to the twin śāla trees and wailed in grief and longing. The Buddha revealed his two feet from within the golden coffin.
The Venerable One addressed the bhikṣus: "The Buddha has already been cremated; the diamond-like relics are no longer our concern. We ought now to hold the council."
"Lest the Eye of the Dharma be severed," he said, and then spoke this verse to announce: "Disciples of the Tathāgata, do not yet enter parinirvāṇa.

Those who have attained supernormal powers (abhijñā) should attend the council. Thereupon, all those who had attained supernormal powers gathered at Vulture Peak Mountain, at the Kūṭāgāra Cave of Piṇḍola.
At that time, Ānanda was unable to join the assembly because his outflows (āsrava) were not yet exhausted; later, he realized the fruit of Arhatship.

He then entered. The Venerable One addressed the assembly, saying: "This bhikṣu Ānanda possesses great wisdom. Whatever Dharma he hears from the Buddha is like water being passed from one vessel to another;
there is nothing left behind. You should invite him to compile the Sūtra Piṭaka. The great assembly remained silent.

(If even such a man of vast learning as this was not permitted to enter the assembly, then those today who have only a slight acquaintance with the scriptures need not concern themselves with their ancestors' shortcomings. As for ordinary people, they are as light as a goose feather; it can be guaranteed that they have not even dreamed of reaching the stage where outflows are exhausted.)
When the council had concluded, the Venerable One reflected upon his own old age and thought it fitting to enter meditative absorption on Mount Kukkuṭapāda to await Maitreya.
He then summoned Ānanda and said: "I shall not remain much longer in this world; I now entrust the True Dharma to you. Guard it well. Listen to my verse:
"Dharmas are by nature the fundamental Dharma; there is no dharma, nor is there any non-dharma. Why..."

Within a single dharma, there is both dharma and non-dharma (like the succession of one lamp from another; such is the receiving of the dharma, such is the entrusting of the dharma. If one speaks of such a dharma, it is more than a thousand miles apart).
The Second Patriarch, Venerable Ānanda, was a native of Rājagṛha. His clan was Kṣatriya; his father was King Droṇodana, and he was the biological younger cousin of the Tathāgata.
He was profoundly learned and widely erudite, possessing unimpeded wisdom. The World-Honored One designated him as the foremost among those who possess *dhāraṇī*.
In Sanskrit he is called Ānanda; here it is translated as "Joyous Celebration" (Qingxi), a name given because he was born on the day the Tathāgata attained enlightenment.
One day he asked Kāśyapa, "Elder brother, apart from the golden-threaded *kāṣāya* robe that the World-Honored One transmitted, what else did he transmit?"
Kāśyapa summoned Ānanda, who responded with an assent. Kāśyapa said, "Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate!

(In the *Jinlan zhuan*, this appears as an independent transmission; summoning Ānanda abruptly seems as though he was unable to endure it. "Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate"—Ānanda was once again deceived by him).

Later, King Ajātaśatru addressed him, saying, "When you enter parinirvāṇa, O Venerable One, I pray that you will grant me leave. As the Venerable One was about to enter nirvāṇa, [he went] to the Ganges River.
In the middle of the stream, he sat cross-legged. King Ajātaśatru and the King of Vaiśālī were both on the riverbank;
they spoke verses to exhort him, entreating him not to enter parinirvāṇa. He replied with a verse: "O two kings, dwell well-composed; do not grieve or mourn in sorrow."
"Nirvana shall be my tranquility, for it is free from all states of existence. He further reflected, "If I were to head toward a single kingdom, the other kingdoms might contend;
I should instead deliver all sentient beings through impartiality. Thereupon, he proceeded into the middle of the Ganges River to enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the mountains, rivers, and great earth shook in six ways. Five hundred rishis from the Snowy Mountains, beholding this auspicious omen, flew through the air and arrived;
they prostrated at the feet of the Venerable One and said, "We shall bear witness to the Buddha-dharma under you, Elder;
we pray that you will bestow upon us your great compassion and deliver us. The Venerable One accepted their request in silence and immediately transformed the Ganges River.

The entire ground became golden. For the sake of that assembly of sages, he preached various Great Dharmas. He then thought of his disciples whom he had previously delivered and liberated, who should now gather together.
In an instant, five hundred arhats descended from the sky; for the sake of these sages, they left the household life and received full ordination.
Within that assembly of sages, there were two arhats: the first was named Śāṇakavāsin, and the second was named Madhyāntika.
"Upagupta, the Venerable One knew you were a vessel for the Dharma and said to you: 'The Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Kāśyapa;
Kāśyapa, having entered meditative absorption, entrusted it to me. Now that I am about to pass away, I entrust it to you in turn. Receive my teaching and listen to these verses:
"The Dharma originally entrusted exists; once entrusted, it is said to be non-existent. Each must awaken to this for themselves. "

Having realized that there is neither existence nor non-existence, he spoke these verses. Having finished speaking the verses, he further entrusted the True Dharma to Śāṇakavāsin and commanded Madhyāntika to propagate the Great Dharma in the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
[The Venerable One leaped into the void and manifested the eighteen transformations; he divided his body into four parts.]

One was offered to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; one was offered to the Palace of the Sāgara Dragon King; one was offered to King Vaiśālī; and one was offered to King Ajātaśatru (each having had a stūpa constructed).
The Third Patriarch, Venerable Śāṇakavāsin, was surnamed Viśākha. His father was Vanavāsin and his mother was Kauśeya; he was a native of the kingdom of Mathurā.
He remained in the womb for six years before being born. In Sanskrit, he is called Śāṇaka, which here means "naturally clothed.
This is the name of a nine-branched, exquisite herb from the Western Regions that grows when a sage is born. When the Venerable One was born, this [herb] appeared.
The *Caoshu* states: Formerly, when the Tathāgata was traveling to convert beings, he arrived at the kingdom of Mathurā.
Seeing a grove of green trees with luxuriant branches and leaves, he said to Ānanda, "This forest is named Uruvilvā.

One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a bhikṣu named Śāṇakavāsin who shall turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma here. A hundred years later, Śāṇakavāsin was indeed born and entered the monastic order.
He attained the Way and received the Dharma-eye of the Venerable Ānanda. Upon reaching this forest, he then subdued two fire-dragons (*nāgas*).

The dragons received the Three Refuges, and he bestowed their land upon him so that he might establish a Brahma-palace. (The *Qinglin xuanyi* records: "When auspicious grasses reveal the time, poison is used to destroy poison; how could the dragons have dared to look? Yet by bestowing the land to build a monastery, they were instead struck down by his seal.")
The Venerable One, having long been engaged in his work for the sake of others, thought of one to whom he might entrust the Dharma.
He soon found Upagupta in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā and took him as an attendant. He then asked Upagupta, "How old are you? He replied, "I am seventeen years old."
The other asked, "Is your body seventeen years old, or is your nature seventeen years old? He replied, "When my teacher’s hair turned white, was it his hair that turned white, or his mind?
The other said, "It was only my hair that turned white; my mind did not turn white. Guptaka said, "My body is seventeen years old, but my nature is not seventeen years old.
The Venerable One knew he was a vessel for the Dharma, and three years later, he finally shaved his head and conferred full ordination upon him. And so...
He entrusted him with the Dharma-eye. The verse of entrustment says: "Neither non-dharma nor mind; Neither no-mind nor dharma.
When speaking of this 'mind-dharma,' This dharma is not a mind-dharma. (Great and small masters have treated these lines as two separate fragments.)
The Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, was a native of the kingdom of Takṣaśilā. His surname was Śūdra and his father’s name was Sumati.

He left home to become a monk at the age of seventeen and realized the fruit [of Arhatship] at twenty. After the Venerable One had attained the Dharma, he traveled through various regions to propagate the teaching.

Upon arriving at the kingdom of Mathurā, the palace of Māra shook violently; Pāpīyas became distressed and terrified, and consequently exerted all his demonic powers to harm the True Dharma. The Venerable One...
As he entered samādhi, he observed the source [of the disturbance]. Māra, watching for an opportunity, secretly took a necklace and fastened it around his neck.

When the Venerable One emerged from concentration, he took three corpses—a human, a dog, and a snake—and transformed them into flower garlands. He addressed Māra with gentle words, and Māra extended his neck to receive them.
The garlands immediately turned into stinking corpses, infested with maggots and putrefying. Māra exerted all his strength, yet in the end he was unable [to remove them].

Having been liberated, he prostrated at the Venerable One’s feet and offered a sincere confession. The Venerable One directed him to take refuge in the Triple Gem, whereupon his flower garland was removed.
Through the Venerable One’s guidance, the greatest number of people realized the fruits of the path; for every person he delivered, he would place a tally-stick in a stone chamber.
The chamber was eighteen cubits long and twelve cubits wide, completely filled [with corpses].
Finally, there was the son of an elder named Gandhamādana, who came to pay homage to the Venerable One and requested ordination. The Venerable One asked him, "Your body has emerged from a tomb."

[The questioner] said, "I have come forth from the household life. He replied, "I have come forth from the household life, not for the sake of body or mind. The Venerable One asked, "If it is not for the sake of body or mind, then who has come forth?
He replied, "As for one who has gone forth from the household life, because there is no self and no 'mine,' there is no self and no 'mine.

Because there is no self and no 'mine,' the mind neither arises nor ceases. That the mind neither arises nor ceases is itself the tasting of the Way. The Buddhas also taste this; the mind has no form or characteristics, and its substance—"

It was likewise so. The Venerable One said, "You shall attain great enlightenment; your mind will naturally penetrate it. You should take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and continue the lineage of the Sages.
He then performed his tonsure and conferred upon him the full precepts (upasampadā). Furthermore, he addressed him, saying, "Your father dreamed of a golden sun at the time of your birth;
you may be named Tiṭṭhaka (Dīrgha-karṇa). The Tathāgata has transmitted the treasury of the Great Dharma-Eye in succession down to this point."
I now entrust this further to you. Listen to my verse: "The mind is itself the original mind; the original mind is not a dharma. If there were dharmas, there would be an original mind;
if it is not the mind, it is not the fundamental dharma."
The Fifth Patriarch, Venerable Diṭṭhako, was a native of the kingdom of Magadha. His original name was Ghoṣila.
At the time of his birth, his father dreamed of a golden sun emerging from the house, its radiance illuminating heaven and earth. Before it stood a great mountain, adorned with various jewels;

from the summit of the mountain, a spring gushed forth, flowing in torrents in four directions. Later, he encountered the Venerable Gupta, who interpreted the dream for him, saying: "As for the jewel mountain..."
"My body is this. The spring gushing forth signifies that the Dharma is inexhaustible. The sun rising from the house represents the sign of your current entry into the Way.
Its illuminating of heaven and earth signifies the transcendence of your wisdom. For this reason, he changed his name; in Sanskrit it is *Tīraka*, which here means "Penetrating True Measure.
Upon hearing this, the Venerable One leaped for joy and recited a verse, saying: "Majestic and lofty, the seven..."
The Jewel Mountain constantly wells forth the spring of wisdom, which turns into the flavor of the True Dharma and is able to deliver all who have the karmic affinity.
The Venerable Kūṭadanta also spoke a verse, saying: "I transmit this Dharma to you; you shall manifest great wisdom. Today, the golden sun emerges from the house."

It shines throughout heaven and earth. When the Venerable One heard the verse, he performed a prostration and received it with reverence. (The fundamental Dharma does not arise from transmission; it arises through the transmission of the fundamental Dharma. Now that which is transmitted is the transmission of the fundamental Dharma.
As for the fundamental Dharma, by whom was it originally transmitted? Later, he arrived in Central India.

In that country there were eight thousand great ṛṣis, with Mucilinda at their head. Hearing that the Venerable One had arrived, they led the assembly to pay him homage. They said to the Venerable One: "In the past, we were born together with you in the Brahma Heaven."
I encountered the seer Asita, who bestowed upon me the methods of the sages; my teacher met a disciple of the One of Ten Powers, who practiced *dhyāna*.
From that time on, our karmic destinies have followed divergent paths for six kalpas. The other said: "That we have been separated for successive kalpas is indeed not in vain."
"Now you may abandon the heterodox and return to the orthodox, thereby entering the Buddha Vehicle. Mīḍhika said, "In the past, the seer Asita bestowed a prediction upon me, saying:
'Six kalpas hence, you shall meet a fellow student and attain the fruit of out-flowlessness. That we have met now—is this not due to a karmic affinity from former lives?
I pray that the Master, out of compassion, will grant me liberation. Thereupon, he was ordained and left the household life. [He] commanded all...
The Holy One bestowed the precepts. The remaining assembly of sages then began to give rise to pride.
The Venerable One manifested great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), whereupon they all simultaneously conceived the bodhicitta and left the household life at once. He then addressed Mucilinda, saying:

"In the past, the Tathāgata secretly entrusted the treasury of the Great Dharma-eye (*mahādharmanetra-kośa*) to Kāśyapa; it was passed down in succession until it reached me. I now entrust it to you. You should..."
He protected and remembered [the assembly], and then spoke this verse: "Thoroughly penetrating the mind of the fundamental dharma, there is neither dharma nor non-dharma.
Awakening is the same as non-awakening; without mind, there is likewise no dharma."

The Sixth Patriarch, Venerable Mīchaka, was a native of Central India. Having transmitted the Dharma, he traveled through various regions for the sake of conversion until he reached the kingdom of Northern India.
There, he beheld auspicious golden clouds upon the battlements of the city walls and sighed, saying, "This is the breath of a person of the Way;
there must surely be a Great Being who shall be my successor. He then entered the city. Amidst the bustling marketplace, he saw a man holding a vessel of wine who came toward him.
He asked, "From where do you come, Master? Where do you intend to go? The Patriarch said, "I come from my own mind; I intend to go nowhere.
The man asked, "Do you recognize this object in my hand? The Patriarch said, "This is a vessel for contact that maintains purity.
The man asked, "Do you recognize me, Master? The Patriarch said, "I do not recognize you. If there were recognition, it would not be me. He spoke to him again, saying, "Try to recognize yourself."
"State your name and clan; I shall show you your original cause. He replied with a verse, saying:
"From immeasurable kalpas until my birth in this land, my original clan was Bharadvāja, and my name was Vasureṣi. The Patriarch said:
"My teacher, Diṭṭhaka, said that when the World-Honored One was formerly traveling through North India, he spoke to Ānanda, saying: 'In this land, after my parinirvāṇa...'"
Three hundred years hence, there will be a sage of the Bharadvāja clan named Vasumitra, who shall be the seventh in the lineage of the Dhyāna patriarchs.
The World-Honored One has prophesied to you: "You should leave the household life. Thereupon, he set down his vessel, prostrated before the Master, and stood to one side, saying:
"I recall a past kalpa when I was once a donor (dānapati) and offered a precious throne to a Tathāgata. That Buddha prophesied to me—"
He said, "In the Dharma of Śākyamuni within this Bhadrakalpa, you shall proclaim the ultimate teaching. This now accords with what the Master has foretold; I pray that you grant me deliverance.
The Patriarch immediately shaved his head and conferred upon him the full precepts of ordination. He then addressed him, saying, "The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is now entrusted to you.
Do not let it be severed. Thereupon he spoke a verse: "No mind exists that can be attained; That which is spoken cannot be called the Dharma."
If one realizes that the mind is not the mind, only then does one understand the mind and mental factors.
The Seventh Patriarch, Venerable Vasumitra, was a native of North India.

He would often wear pure robes while carrying vessels of wine, wandering through the streets and alleys, sometimes chanting and sometimes whistling; people regarded him as mad. However, upon meeting the Venerable Miśraka, he proclaimed [the truth] as follows:
Record of Comings and Goings: Reflecting upon my past affinities, I cast myself as a worthy vessel to leave the household life and receive the Dharma.

While traveling to propagate the teachings, I arrived at the kingdom of Kāmarūpa and extensively promoted Buddhist activities. Before the Dharma seat, there suddenly appeared a wise man who declared his name to be Buddhanandi.
"Now let us debate the meaning of the Dharma," [Nan-ti] said. The Master replied, "If you are benevolent, there is no need for debate; if you engage in debate, you are not benevolent.

If you intend to debate over meanings, it will ultimately not be a discussion of the true meaning. Nan-ti realized that the Master’s argument was superior and submitted with sincere respect, saying, "I wish to seek the Way."
[He bestowed upon him] the flavor of the nectar of immortality. The Patriarch then granted him the tonsure and conferred the full precepts.

He further addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, I now entrust to you. You must protect and uphold it. Thereupon, he spoke this verse: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space."
He demonstrated the dharma that is equal to space. When he realized the state of space, there was neither "is" nor "non-dharma.
At that time, Brahmā, Śakra, and the hosts of devas all came together to pay homage and spoke these verses: "O Ancestor of the Sages of the Bhadrakalpa, you shall occupy the seventh position.
Venerable One, have compassion for us; we pray that you will proclaim the Buddha-ground. The Venerable One arose from samādhi and demonstrated—
The assembly said, "The Dharma we have attained is non-existent; if one speaks of the stage of Buddhahood, it is free from both existence and non-existence.
Having spoken thus, they returned to samādhi and manifested the signs of nirvāṇa. Nandi then rose from his seat and erected a stūpa of the seven precious jewels to enshrine his entire body.
This was the year of the Xinwei cycle, the nineteenth year of the Reign of Stability (Dingwang).
The Eighth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhanandi, was a native of the kingdom of Kāmarūpa. His clan name was Gautama.

He possessed a fleshly protuberance upon his crown and was endowed with swift and unimpeded eloquence. Having received the Dharma from Venerable Vasumitra, he traveled to the kingdom of Tika to propagate the teachings.
At the house of Viśāla, he observed a white light ascending from the roof and said to his disciples, "There is a sage in this house. His mouth—
He remained without speech. He was a true vessel for the Mahāyāna. He did not travel along the four crossroads; he knew that contact with the ear was defilement.

When the elder came out and paid his respects, he asked, "What do you require? The Patriarch said, "I am seeking an attendant. The elder said, "I have a son named Buddhabhadra. He is already fifty years old;
he has never spoken a word from his mouth, nor has he ever set foot upon the ground. The Patriarch said, "If it is as you describe," [he will serve me].
"Truly my disciple. When Puṇyamitra heard this, he rose immediately to prostrate himself and spoke in verse:
"My parents are not my kin; who is the most intimate kin? The Buddhas are not my path; who is the supreme path?
The Patriarch answered him in verse: "What you say accords with the mind; parents cannot be compared to it. Your practice accords with the Way; the minds of all Buddhas are [one with yours]."
"It is so. To seek an external Buddha with attributes is not in accord with you. If you wish to recognize your original mind, it is neither joined nor separate.
After Vovada heard this verse, he immediately took seven steps. The Patriarch said, "This child encountered a Buddha in the past; his compassionate vows are vast and great.
Fearing that his parents' affection would make him difficult to relinquish, he remained silent and did not walk. The elder then relinquished him.

He left the household life. His master then conferred upon him the full precepts (*upasampadā*) and, transmitting the Dharma, spoke this verse: "Space has neither interior nor exterior; The nature of the mind is likewise so.

If one thoroughly understands space, One penetrates the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*). [With these words, he immediately knew where to return; he did not fail the flesh-crown (*uṣṇīṣa*) he was born with.]

The Ninth Patriarch, Vajramitra, was a native of the country of Tika. His secular surname was Viśāla. While traveling to transform beings in Central India, he encountered an elder named Gandhacchattra who brought his son with him.
Gazing upon him in worship, the elder said, "This child remained in the womb for sixty years (the *Zhengzong* edition reads sixteen).
Once there was a rishi who remarked that this boy’s skeletal features were unlike those of ordinary men; now he has met the World-Honored One."

"You may let him go forth and renounce the world. The Patriarch then shaved his head. At the moment of the *karmavācanā* ceremony, auspicious light illuminated the seat, and thirty *śarīra* relics miraculously appeared before them.
From then on, he practiced with such diligence that he forgot all fatigue. Before long, the Patriarch transmitted the Dharma to him, speaking this verse:
"The True Principle is originally nameless; To manifest the True Principle, one must employ names. Having received the true and real Dharma, It is neither true nor false."
False. Having transmitted the Dharma, he immediately entered the samādhi of cessation and attained parinirvāṇa.
The assembly cremated him with fragrant oil and sandalwood, collected his relics, and erected a stūpa at Nālandā Monastery. This was in the year Jiǎyīn of King Jing’s reign.
The Tenth Patriarch, Venerable Śrīkṣetra, was a native of Central India; his clan name is unknown. He remained in the womb for sixty years.
On the eve of his birth, his mother dreamed of a white elephant carrying a precious throne, upon which rested a bright pearl, entering her chamber;

thereupon he was born. At birth, divine light illuminated the room and his body emitted a wondrous fragrance. Upon reaching adulthood, although he consumed grain-based food, it passed through him without any waste or residue. His original name was...

He was difficult to give birth to. Later, he served the Ninth Patriarch, attending him at his side without ever sleeping; it is said that his ribs never touched the mat, and thus he was called the Venerable Vakṣa.
When he first arrived at the city of Pāṭaliputra, he rested beneath a tree and pointed to the ground with his right hand, declaring to the assembly:
"When this ground turns golden in color, a sage shall enter this assembly. As soon as he finished speaking, the ground turned golden. At that time...
There was a son of a householder named Pūrṇayaśas, who stood before him with palms joined. The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from?
He replied, "My mind does not go anywhere. The Patriarch said, "Where do you dwell? He replied, "My mind does not abide anywhere. The Patriarch said, "Is your mind not settled?
He replied, "The Buddhas are likewise so. The Patriarch said, "Are you not the Buddhas? He replied, "The Buddhas are also not [the Buddhas]. Thereupon, the Patriarch ordained him.
He left the household life and further perfected the categories of the precepts. Then, entrusting the Dharma, he spoke this verse: "The true essence is naturally real;

Because it is real, there is the principle of explanation. Having realized the Dharma of true reality, There is neither practice nor cessation. Having entrusted the Dharma, he immediately manifested supernatural transformations and entered nirvana.
He transformed into fire to cremate himself. The fourfold assembly each took up his relics in their robes and constructed stupas at various locations.
(Not letting his side touch the mat; his backbone was cast of iron; he trampled the golden ground and pierced through the pivot of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

The eleventh patriarch, Venerable Pūrṇāśaya, was a native of the country of Pāṭaliputra. His secular surname was Gautama. Having met the Venerable Upagupta, he was subsequently bestowed with the Dharma.
The patriarch’s teachings reached immeasurable beings, and those who attained the fruit numbered five hundred. Later, he arrived at Pāṭaliputra.
In the kingdom of Aṅga, there was an elder who came to attend that assembly. Āryadeva said to the multitude, "Do you recognize this person who has come?
The Buddha prophesied that the noble Mātr̥ceṭa shall succeed to my Dharma. Thereupon, Mātr̥ceṭa paid his respects and asked:

"I wish to recognize the Buddha. Which one is it? The Patriarch said, "If you wish to recognize the Buddha, that which you do not recognize is it. He asked, "Since I do not recognize the Buddha, how can I know it is him? The Patriarch said, "Since you do not recognize the Buddha, how can you know it is not? He said, "This is the meaning of the saw. The Patriarch said, "That is the meaning of the wood. The Patriarch asked, "What is the meaning of the saw? He replied, "It cuts through equally with the Master. The Patriarch said, "You have cut yourself. He asked, "How so? The Patriarch said, "Because you take me to be the same as the saw. He asked, "What is the meaning of the wood? The Patriarch said, "The saw is in it. He asked, "Is there anything else besides the saw and the wood? The Patriarch said, "There is. He asked, "What is it? The Patriarch said, "I am. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'I'? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'I' is that there is no 'I'. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'no 'I'? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'no 'I'' is that there is no 'no 'I''. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'no 'no 'I''? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'no 'no 'I'' is that there is no 'no 'no 'I''. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'I''? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'I'' is that there is no 'no 'no 'no 'I''. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I'' is that there is no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I'' is that there is no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I'' is that there is no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I'' is that there is no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I'' is that there is no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I'' is that there is no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I'' is that there is no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I'' is that there is no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I'' is that there is no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I'' is that there is no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I'' is that there is no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I'' is that there is no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I'' is that there is no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I'' is that there is no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I'' is that there is no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I''? The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'I'' is that there is no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no 'no
Aśvaghoṣa then asked, "What is the meaning of 'wood'? The Patriarch replied, "You have been liberated by me.
Aśvaghoṣa attained sudden enlightenment and subsequently requested ordination. The Patriarch said to the assembly, "This Great Being was formerly King Viśākhā.
Because there was a class of people in his kingdom who were naked like horses, the king exercised his supernatural powers and divided his body into silkworms."
He clothed him with robes. Later, he was born in Central India; because the horse-man (Aśvaghosa) felt such deep longing that it neighed piteously, he was named Aśvaghoṣa.
The Tathāgata had made a prediction: six hundred years after his parinirvāṇa, Aśvaghoṣa would, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, subdue and defeat those of heterodox paths.
The number of people saved is immeasurable. Now is precisely the right time. He then transmitted the verse of the Dharma, saying: "Delusion and awakening are like concealment and manifestation;

light and darkness are never separate from one another. Now I transmit this dharma of concealment and manifestation—it is neither one, nor is it two. (Its true meaning is blazingly clear, without error or mistake.
What is there to lament with such sorrowful cries? It is both two and not-two.)"
The twelfth patriarch, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa, was a native of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. He was also named Saṃgharakṣita;
he was so named because his cultivated and unconditioned merits were preeminent and most excellent.

Having received the Dharma from the Venerable Yaśas, he later turned the wonderful wheel of the Dharma in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. Suddenly, an old man prostrated himself on the ground before him. The Patriarch said:
The assembly said, "This is no ordinary person; there must be some extraordinary sign. As they finished speaking, [the figure] vanished.
Suddenly, a golden-colored man emerged from the earth, who then transformed into a woman. She pointed her right hand toward the Patriarch and spoke this verse:

"I prostrate to the Honored Elder, Who shall receive the prediction of the Tathāgata. Now, upon this very ground, You proclaim and disseminate the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha). Having spoken the verse, she vanished in an instant.

However, he did not see anything. The Patriarch said, "A demon is about to come to contend with me for strength. After a short while, wind and rain arrived violently, and heaven and earth grew dark and gloomy.
The Patriarch said, "It is certain that the demon has come; I shall eliminate him.

He then pointed into the air, and a great golden dragon appeared, manifesting its majestic spiritual power and shaking the mountains and peaks. The Patriarch remained solemn upon his seat, and the demonic disturbances were instantly extinguished.
After seven days had passed, there was a small insect, as large as a mayfly, that hid its form beneath the Master’s seat.

The Master took it up with his hand and showed it to the assembly, saying, "This is a transformation of Māra, coming to eavesdrop upon my Dharma. He released it to let it go, but the Māra could not move.
The Master addressed him, saying, "If you simply take refuge in the Triple Gem, you shall immediately attain supernatural powers. Thereupon, he returned to his original form.
He performed prostrations and repented. The Patriarch asked, "What is your name, and how large is your retinue?
He replied, "My name is Kambala, and I have three thousand followers. The Patriarch said, "Exerting your supernatural powers to the full, what transformations can you perform?
He replied, "I could transform a vast ocean; that would be a very minor feat. The Patriarch asked, "Can you transform the ocean of nature? He asked, "What is the ocean of nature? I—
He had never known this before. The Patriarch then explained the ocean of nature (*dharmatā-samudra*) to him, saying: "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all established upon it;

the three samādhis and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are manifested through it. Upon hearing these words, Kāpimāra gave rise to faith and, together with three thousand followers, requested ordination.
The Patriarch then summoned five hundred arhats to confer the full precepts (*upasaṃpadā*) upon them, and further addressed them, saying:
The Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury is now to be entrusted to you. Listen to these verses: "Manifestation and concealment are the fundamental Dharma;

Light and darkness are originally not two. Now I entrust this Dharma of realization, Neither to be grasped nor to be abandoned. [He reveals his claws and fangs in the air, subduing the great illusory enemy.]
Having attained a measure of supernatural powers (through which both Māras and Buddhas are brought to rest), the Thirteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kāpimāra, was a native of the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra.

Initially a non-Buddhist, he had three thousand disciples and was well-versed in various heterodox doctrines. Later, he received the Dharma from the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa and led his followers to Western India.
That king had a crown prince named Meghasvāmin. Hearing the Venerable One’s name, he invited him to the palace to provide offerings.

As the Patriarch was about to reach a stone cave, an old man dressed in plain white robes came out, joined his palms in greeting, and asked him, "What is it that you seek? The Master stopped. He replied, "In the past, I was once a bhikṣu who greatly delighted in stillness and seclusion.

A novice bhikṣu frequently came to request instruction, but I grew weary of responding to him and conceived thoughts of resentment. When my life ended, I fell into the body of a python and have dwelt in this cave for a thousand years.
Having now encountered the Venerable One and been able to hear the Dharma of the precepts, I have come to express my gratitude. The Patriarch asked:
He asked, "Who else dwells on this mountain? He replied, "Ten li from here, there is a great tree that provides shade for five hundred great nāgas.
This king of trees is named Nāgārjuna; he has frequently preached the Dharma for the assembly of nāgas, and I too have listened to and received it."
The Patriarch then proceeded with his disciples to that place. Nāgārjuna came out to meet him and said, "This deep mountain is secluded and desolate, a dwelling place for dragons and pythons.

Most Virtuous One, how is it that you have deigned to trouble your divine feet? The Patriarch replied, "I am no one of supreme status; I have come to visit a worthy man. Nāgārjuna thought silently to himself:
"Has this master attained the nature of certainty? Is he clear-sighted regarding the Way? Is he a Great Sage who shall succeed to the True Vehicle?"
The Patriarch said, "Although you spoke with your mind, I have already known it with my mind. Simply prepare for ordination; why worry that I am not a sage?
Having heard this, Nāgārjuna repented and apologized. The Patriarch immediately granted him ordination and liberation, along with five hundred dragon followers, all of whom received full precepts.
He spoke again, saying: "The Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury is now entrusted to you. Listen attentively to these verses:
'The dharma that is neither hidden nor manifest—this is called the true limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). To awaken to this dharma of non-hiddenness and non-manifestation is neither folly nor wisdom.

[Though] the great python took refuge and the venomous dragon received the precepts—such powers of spiritual penetration and wisdom were indeed not lacking—yet they had not even dreamed of 'the dharma that is neither hidden nor manifest.'"
The Fourteenth Patriarch, Venerable Nāgārjuna, was also known as Nāgasena. In his youth, he was able to recite the four Vedas;

as he grew, he became proficient in all arts and possessed divine eloquence. He left the household life and entered a stone cave, where he dwelt among the dragon trees (nāga-vṛkṣa) and became a refuge for the dragon hosts.
There he met the Venerable Māra, from whom he received the transmission of the Dharma. Later, he traveled to South India, where the people of that country were largely devoted to [heretical views].
Fuyue. The Patriarch preached the Dharma for him. Fuyue said to his companions, "Among men, there is one whose meritorious karma is foremost in the world.
We speak in vain of Buddha-nature; who can truly behold it? The Patriarch said, "If you wish to see Buddha-nature, you must first eliminate your ego-conceit (*asmimāna*.
