The deceased was not reborn. Having heard that the principle [of the Patriarch] was superior, they all returned to their original resolve.

The Patriarch then manifested a body of sovereign mastery upon his seat, like the orb of the full moon; yet the entire assembly heard only the sound of the Dharma and could not perceive the form of the Patriarch.
Among the assembly was the son of an elder named Kanadeva, who asked the crowd, "Do you recognize this sign? The crowd replied, "It is something our eyes have never beheld."
"How can we distinguish this? Deva replied, "This is the Venerable One manifesting the essence and form of Buddha-nature to show us.
How do we know this? It is because through the signless samādhi, his form is like the full moon; the meaning of Buddha-nature is vast, empty, and luminous.
As soon as he finished speaking, the wheel-mark vanished, and he returned to his original seat, whereupon he spoke this verse: "The body manifests the full moon..."
The marks manifest the essence of all Buddhas; the preaching of the Dharma has no fixed form, for its function is to discern that which is neither sound nor color.

When the assembly heard these verses, they suddenly realized non-arising and all vowed to leave the household life in their quest for liberation. The Patriarch then shaved their heads and commanded the various sages to bestow full ordination upon them.
He composed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, and the *Dvādaśanikāya-śāstra*, transmitting them to the world. Later, he entrusted the Dharma...
Regarding Kanadeva, the verse of the transmission of the Dharma says: "To clarify the principle of concealment and manifestation, one speaks of the logic of liberation.

Regarding the Dharma, the mind does not grasp it; there is neither anger nor joy. (The moon disc appears on the spot; its nature and meaning are vast, empty, and luminous. It pierces through thousands of miles; it is neither form nor sound.)"
The Fifteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kanadeva, was a native of South India. His secular surname was Viśrāva.
Initially, he sought to cultivate meritorious deeds while simultaneously seeking to master debate. Later, he went to visit the Great Being Nāgārjuna.

As he approached the gate, Nāgārjuna, recognizing him as a man of wisdom, first sent his attendant to place a bowl filled with water before the seat. Upon seeing this, the Venerable [Kanadeva] immediately...
He cast a single needle into it and it moved forward; they joyfully reached a state of mutual accord. After he had received the Dharma, he arrived at the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
There was an elder there named Brahmāyuṣmat who gave up his second son, Rāhulabhadra, to follow the Master into the homeless life. The Patriarch said:
"In the past, the Tathāgata prophesied that this boy would become a great teacher during the second five-hundred-year period. Now we have met."

This was due to his past karmic causes. He immediately had his hair shaved (Holding the sword of heaven and earth in hand, with the banner of sun and moon stored in his breast; having already displayed his wondrous capacity before the opportune moment, how could Buddhas and patriarchs fathom him?).
In the household of Jingde there was a garden tree from which mushrooms grew like fungi; their flavor was most excellent. Only Jingde and his second son, Luoda, were able to take and eat them.
Once taken, they would grow back immediately; when they were exhausted, they would grow again. None of the other relatives were able to see them.
Kātyāyana knew of his past causes and showed him [the mushrooms], saying: "In the past, you once made offerings to a bhikṣu. This bhikṣu’s insight into the Path was not yet clear;

because he had received your offerings in faith in vain, he was reborn as these wooden mushrooms. It was solely because you and your son made offerings with such sincerity that you were able to enjoy them.

(The needle thrown into the bowl, beholding the lunar disc—all these were the causes for the wooden mushrooms; he recognized the bhikṣu’s precepts. Truly, it is like piercing the brain to enter the glue-pot, or striking the grass and being startled by the snake. Up to this point...

In the city of Pāṭaliputra, [the Master] heard that various non-Buddhists intended to obstruct the Buddha-dharma. Having deliberated on this for some time, the Patriarch took up a long banner and entered into their assembly.
They asked the Patriarch, "Why do you not go forward? The Patriarch replied, "Why do you not stay behind? They said, "You appear to be a lowly person.
The Patriarch replied, "You appear to be a noble person. They asked, "What Dharma do you understand? The Patriarch replied, "You..."
The other did not understand. He said, "I wish to attain Buddhahood. The Patriarch said, "I have certainly attained Buddhahood. The other said, "It is not fitting for you to attain it.
The Patriarch said, "Originally I say that I have attained it; you truly have not attained it. The other said, "Since you have not attained it, why do you say you have?
The Patriarch said, "Because you possess the notion of 'self,' you therefore do not attain it. I am without self or the notion of self; therefore, I naturally attain it."
His arguments being thus defeated, he asked the Patriarch, "What is your name? The Patriarch replied, "My name is Kāṇadeva.

Since he had long heard of the Patriarch's reputation, he repented his errors and offered his thanks. At that time, those in the assembly still raised various challenges and difficulties, but the Patriarch refuted them with unimpeded eloquence;
consequently, they all submitted and took refuge in him. He then addressed his senior disciple, Rāhulabhadra, and entrusted the Dharma to him.

it has neither end nor beginning. In the Gengchen year of Emperor Wen of the Han dynasty, his body emitted eight rays of light as he returned to nirvana.

There was a river there called Suvarṇodaka (Golden Water), whose taste was exceptionally fine; in its midstream, the reflections of five Buddhas appeared.
The Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying: "The source of this river is five hundred *li* away. There dwells the holy one Saṃghanandin."

The Seventeenth Patriarch, Venerable Saṃghanandin, was the son of King Ratnavyuha of the city of Śrāvastī.
He was able to speak as soon as he was born and would often praise the deeds of the Buddha. At the age of seven, he grew weary of worldly pleasures and addressed his parents with a verse, saying:
"I bow my head to my Greatly Compassionate Father; I pay homage to my Mother of Bone and Blood. I now wish to leave the home-life; I pray you will have pity on me.

His parents tried to dissuade him firmly, but he subsequently refused to eat for an entire day. They finally permitted him to leave the home-life while remaining at home, and he was given the name Seng.
Kāṇḍī reappointed the śramaṇa Śāṇakavāsin as his teacher. For nineteen years, he never once grew weary or indolent.
He often thought to himself, "I dwell within a royal palace; why have I left the household life? One night, a divine light shone down upon him, revealing a level path.
Without realizing it, he walked slowly for about ten *li* until he reached a great cliff, where there was a stone cave.

Thereupon, he remained in tranquil seclusion within. When the father lost his son, he immediately banished Śāṇakavāsin from the country and went abroad in search of him, but did not know where he was.
After ten years had passed, the Patriarch, having received the Dharma and the prediction of his attainment, traveled to the kingdom of Mathurā to spread the teaching.

Suddenly, a cool breeze swept over the bodies and minds of the assembly, bringing a sense of joy and comfort such as they had never experienced before, yet they did not know its cause. The Patriarch said, "This is the Way."
"This is the wind of virtue. There must be a sage appearing in the world to continue the ancestral lamp.

Having finished speaking, he used his supernatural powers to lead the great assembly on a journey through mountains and valleys. Within the time it takes to eat a meal, they arrived at the foot of a peak.

He said to the assembly, "On the summit of this peak there is purple cloud like a canopy; a sage dwells here. He and the assembly then wandered about for a long while until they saw a mountain cottage.

A young boy, holding a round mirror, went straight before the Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, “How old are you? He replied, “One hundred years. The Patriarch said, “You are still quite young; why do you say you are one hundred? The boy said, “I do not understand the principle; I am truly one hundred years old. The Patriarch asked, “Are you skilled in the pivotal point? The boy said, “The Buddha said: ‘If a person lives for a hundred years, yet does not understand the pivotal point of all Buddhas, it is not as good as living for a single day and attaining such understanding. The Patriarch said, “You have attained it. The boy then bowed and departed. The Patriarch then called out to him, and the boy turned his head. The Patriarch said, “What is this? The boy said, “It is not that I do not know; I simply do not speak of it. The Patriarch said, “You have attained it. The boy then bowed and departed. Later, the Patriarch told the assembly, “This boy has attained the pivotal point of all Buddhas. The boy was named Huairang. He later became the Sixth Patriarch. On the very day he was born, he attained definitive understanding. The Patriarch asked, "What does that which is in your hand signify?
The boy replied, "The great perfect mirror of all Buddhas; within and without, it is free from flaw or obscuration. Two people see it together; the eye of the mind is identical in both.

When his parents heard their son’s words, they immediately relinquished him so that he might leave the household life. The Patriarch took him to his own dwelling and conferred upon him the full precepts.
[The transmission] was completed. He was named Gayāśata. On another occasion, he heard the sound of wind blowing through the palace bells.

His master asked him, "Is it the bells that ring, or is it the wind? He replied, "It is neither the wind nor the bells that ring; it is my own mind that rings. The master said, "And who is it that possesses this mind?
He replied, "Because both are utterly quiescent. The master said, "Excellent, excellent! Who else but you could succeed to my Way? Thereupon, he transmitted the Dharma to him.

The verse on the eye says: "In the ground of the mind, there is fundamentally no arising; the ground arises from conditions. Condition and seed do not obstruct one another; so too it is with flowers and fruit.
Having thus entrusted the Dharma, he immediately grasped a tree with his right hand and passed away. The great assembly erected a stupa beneath the tree.
[He cast aside worldly glory and sat in tranquil seclusion within a stone cave; yet enmity and debt followed him in pursuit, just as a magnet attracts iron.]
The eighteenth patriarch, Venerable Gayasata, was a native of the country of Mathura. His surname was Udrayana; his father was Devavarma and his mother was Bhadra.
She once dreamed that a great deity held up a mirror, and consequently she became pregnant. He was born after seven days, his body as translucent as lapis lazuli.
He never required washing or bathing, yet he was naturally fragrant and pure. From childhood he delighted in seclusion and tranquility; his speech was not like that of ordinary people.
As a youth, he took a mirror and went out for a stroll. There he met the Venerable Nandī and received ordination. Later, leading his disciples, he arrived at the kingdom of Mahācīna.
Seeing an unusual aura over a Brahmin’s house, the Patriarch was about to enter when the householder Kumāralata asked, "Who are these followers?
The Patriarch replied, "We are disciples of the Buddha. Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, Kumāralata’s spirit was suddenly stirred. He then...
At that time, he had closed the door. After a long while, Sengzhu knocked on the door. Luoduo said, "There is no one in this house. Sengzhu asked, "Who is it that answers 'no'?
Upon hearing these words, Luoduo realized he was an extraordinary person; he quickly opened the door to welcome him. Sengzhu said, "In the past, the World-Honored One made a prophecy:
'One thousand years after my parinirvāṇa, a Great Being shall appear in the kingdom of Mo-zhi (Mūlasthāna) to propagate and uphold the profound [Dharma].'"

[The Buddha] transformed [him]. Now you have encountered me; you should respond to this auspicious fortune. Thereupon, Kumārajīva awakened to the knowledge of his past lives and devotedly entered the monastic order.

Having received full ordination, [the Buddha] entrusted him with a verse of the Dharma, saying: "When there is a seed and the ground of the mind, through causes and conditions, the sprout can emerge."
Unimpeded within conditions, whether arising or not arising; having transmitted the Dharma, he leaped into the void and manifested eighteen transformations.
Entering the Fire-Light Samādhi, he spontaneously incinerated his own body. The assembly collected the relics and erected a stupa. (The mechanism of all Buddhas, the intent of the wind-bells:
even if one can explain the principles with perfect clarity, one cannot avoid having an iron collar placed around one's neck.)
The nineteenth patriarch, Venerable Kumāralāta, was the son of a Brahmin from the kingdom of Greater Yuezhi.
Later, he arrived in the kingdom of Central India, where there was a Mahāsattva named Jayata who asked him: "In my family, our parents have long been faithful believers in the Triple Gem;
yet they have frequently been afflicted by chronic illnesses, and whatever we undertake never turns out as we wish. Furthermore, our neighbors have long been Caṇḍālas..."
The executioner replied, "I take killing as my profession and have always been physically brave and strong; our work has been harmonious—what good fortune for him, and what crime have I committed?
The Patriarch said, "Why should you doubt this? Furthermore, the retribution for good and evil occurs across three periods of time.

Ordinary people see only that the benevolent die young while the violent live long, or that the rebellious meet with good fortune while the righteous suffer misfortune; they then claim that cause and effect do not exist and that merit and retribution are empty. They fail to realize that [retribution is like] a shadow..."
The resonance follows the sound; there is not even the slightest discrepancy between them. Even if they were to pass through hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, they would never perish.
At that time, having heard these words, Śāṇakavāsin was suddenly relieved of his doubts. The Patriarch said:

"Although you have already gained faith in the three karmas, you have not yet clarified that karma arises from delusion, delusion exists dependent on consciousness, consciousness depends on non-awakening, and non-awakening depends on the mind. The mind is fundamentally pure."
There is no arising or ceasing; no fabrication; no retribution; no victory or defeat. It is profoundly still and vibrantly luminous.
If you enter this Dharma-gate, you may be one with all Buddhas. All that is good or evil, conditioned or unconditioned, is like a dream or an illusion.
Upon hearing these words and grasping their meaning, Śāṇakavāsin immediately awakened his latent wisdom and earnestly sought to leave the household life. Having received full ordination, he—
The Patriarch said, “The time for my parinirvāṇa has now arrived. You shall succeed me in carrying forth the traces of my transformation. The verse for the transmission of the Dharma-eye says:

‘In the fundamental nature, there is originally no birth; It is spoken only in response to those who seek it. Since there is nothing to be attained within the Dharma, Why harbor doubts about what is or is not resolved?
[Attaining the power of prajñā, he pointed directly at the scene, touching his own nostrils. Space was completely filled.]”
The twentieth patriarch, Venerable Jayata, was a native of Northern India. His wisdom was profound and deep;
his transformative teachings were immeasurable. Later, he arrived at the city of Rājagṛha to propagate the sudden teaching (*tun-jiao*). There, the assembly of students valued debate above all else.

Their leader was named Vaśu-bandhu, who constantly ate but one meal a day, never lay down to sleep, and performed prostrations to the Buddha during the six periods of the day, remaining pure and undefiled.

Yaoxuan was sought after by the multitude. When the Patriarch intended to convert him, he first asked the assembly: "This wandering mendicant, Bianxing, is able to cultivate the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
Can he attain the Way of the Buddha? The assembly replied, "Our teacher is diligent; why should he not be capable?
The Patriarch said, "Your teacher is far removed from the Way. Even if he were to undergo ascetic practices for kalpas as numerous as dust motes, they would all be the root of delusion."
The assembly asked, "What virtues and conduct does the Venerable One possess that he should disparage our Master? The Patriarch said, "I do not seek the Way, yet I am not inverted.
I do not prostrate to the Buddha, yet I am not disrespectful. I do not sit in meditation, yet I am not indolent.
I do not eat only once a day, yet I do not eat indiscriminately. I am not contented, yet I have no greed. My mind harbors no expectations; this is what I call [the Way]."

He replied, "The Way. Upon hearing this, Sarvakāmin attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and joyfully offered praise. The Patriarch further addressed the assembly, saying, "Do you understand my words?
The reason I acted thus was because his aspiration for the Way was so fervent. Now, if a string is too tight, it will snap;
therefore, I did not praise him, so as to cause him to abide in the ground of peace and bliss and enter the wisdom of all Buddhas. He then spoke again to Sarvakāmin:
"I have just confronted the assembly and humiliated you, O Benevolent One; surely this must cause distress in your heart?
Viśvāmitra replied, "When I hear harsh words, I regard them as the wind or an echo. How much more so now that I have heard the unsurpassed nectar—would I instead give rise to feverish affliction?"
"I only pray that you, in your great compassion, will instruct me with the wondrous Way. The Patriarch said, "You have long planted manifold virtues and shall succeed to my lineage.
Listen to this verse of mine: 'In a single word, one accords with the unborn; it is identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm.

If one can understand it thus, one will thoroughly penetrate both phenomena and principle. [At these words, his innate wisdom suddenly awakened; he silently realized the source. He realized that the essence is fundamentally unborn—what dharma could there be to explain? It is most simple and most easy, most honored and most precious, passing over the crowns of a thousand sages.]

Inconceivable in both the mundane and supramundane realms, with a single snap of the fingers one perfectly accomplishes the eighty thousand gates and transcends directly into the stage of the Tathāgata.
The twenty-first patriarch, Vasiṣṭha, was a native of Rājagṛha. At the age of fifteen, he paid homage to the arhat Prabhāsa and left the household life.
Moved by his sincerity, the Bodhisattva Vibhāṣā conferred the precepts upon him. He traveled to Nādikā to propagate the teachings.
In that country, there was a king named Constant Sovereignty (Nityeśvara). He had two sons: the elder was named Mahāla, and the younger was named Maṣula.
The king asked his grandfather, "How does the local custom of Rājagṛha differ from this? The grandfather replied, "Three Buddhas have appeared in that place in the past;
now, in Your Majesty’s kingdom, there are two teachers who provide guidance. The king asked, "Who are these two teachers? The grandfather replied, "The Buddha has prophesied..."
In the second five-hundred-year period, there will be two great beings of supernatural power who leave the household life to succeed the Sage. One is the King’s second son, Maṇḍara;
though my virtue is meager, I shall be the other. Initially, in the kingdom of Nādi, there was a wicked elephant that caused harm.
Nāla was born, and the elephant’s affliction ceased; it has now been thirty years. People still did not know why the affliction had ceased.
While the King was conversing with the Elder, a messenger suddenly reported that more than ten thousand giant elephants were pressing against the city walls.

The King was distressed by this, but the Elder said, "If Nāla comes out, the calamity will be resolved. The King then tested this by ordering Nāla to come out; Nāla accordingly emerged and headed toward the south of the city.
The elephant struck his belly and let out a great roar; the city shook, and the herd of elephants fell prostrate. In an instant, they all fled and dispersed.

At this, the people finally realized that their thirty years of peace had been due to Nala. The King, filled with great reverence and faith, commanded Nala to renounce the world according to his grandfather’s tradition.

His grandfather immediately conferred the full precepts upon him and gave him the verse of the transmission of the Dharma, which said: "Foam and illusions are equally unimpeded; how can one not understand this?"
Awakening: to penetrate the Dharma within it—neither now nor ancient (to know where to rest; black jade and white iron, he speaks directly at one’s head; bright moon and cold snow).
The twenty-second patriarch, Venerable Mañjarī, was of the Kṣatriya caste. His father was King Nityeśvara.
Having received the command of the venerable Paṇḍu, the patriarch subsequently left the household life. After transmitting the Dharma, he arrived in the kingdom of Mo-chih (Mūlasthāna).

Hele-na (Kakuda) and Bao-yin (Ratnamudrā) welcomed the patriarch to the royal palace to provide offerings. On another day, Hele-na asked the patriarch: "By what karmic conditions do I possess [this merit]?"
He thereby moved the flock of cranes. The Patriarch said, "In the fourth kalpa, you shall always be a bhikṣu.
You must go to the assembly at the Dragon Palace; your disciples all wish to follow you. However, observe that among these five hundred followers, not one is worthy of the sublime offerings.
At that time, the disciples said, "Our Master has often preached the Dharma: 'That which is equal in food is also equal in the Dharma. Now..."
"If it were not so, how could there be such a thing as a sage? You have merely caused him to attend this assembly and sit here to consume food in vain; his retribution is that he has become a bird.
Because of the karmic affinity between teacher and disciple from former lives, he now follows you. Helunuo asked, "By what skillful means can he be brought to liberation?"

The Patriarch said: "I possess the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure, which is the Tathāgatagarbha. In the past, the World-Honored One entrusted it to Mahākāśyapa, and it was passed down successively until it reached me.
I now entrust it to you; you must be able to transmit it without interruption. Even those flocks of cranes shall be aided by this toward liberation.
Receive my teaching, and listen as I recite this verse: 'The mind turns following the myriad objects; where it turns, it is truly profound. Following [the objects]...'

Having realized the nature within the flow of existence, there is neither joy nor sorrow. When the flock of cranes heard this verse, they flew away with cries. (Born into a royal palace, he attained these profound mysteries;
responding to the Buddha’s prophetic prediction, he divided the lamp to transform and guide others. The flock of cranes attained liberation, like fire meeting dry wood.)
The twenty-third patriarch, Venerable Hargana, was a native of the country of Moji (Yuezhi). His clan name was Brahmin; his father was Qiansheng, and his mother was Jinguang.
Having prayed to the golden pillars of the Seven Buddhas for a son, she dreamed that atop Mount Sumeru a divine child appeared holding a golden ring and saying, "I have come.
When he was born, the heavens rained down flowers. At the age of twenty-two, he left the household life and dwelt in a forest.
For nine years he recited the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which moved a flock of cranes to follow him. At thirty, he attained the Dharma and traveled to Central India to propagate his teachings.
There was one named Siṃha who took refuge in him and asked, "I wish to seek the Way; how should I apply my mind?

The Patriarch said, "If you wish to seek the Way, there is no place for the mind to be applied. Siṃha asked, "If there is no application of the mind, who performs the work of a Buddha? The Patriarch said:
"If you have any purposeful activity, it is not merit. If you are without action, that is itself the work of the Buddha.
The Sūtra says: "The merit I have performed is without the notion of 'mine'. Upon hearing these words, Śiṃha immediately entered the wisdom of the Buddha.

At that time, the Patriarch suddenly pointed toward the northeast and asked, "What kind of atmospheric phenomenon is this? Śiṃha replied, "I see a vapor like a white rainbow piercing through [the sky]."
Within the space between heaven and earth, there were again five paths of black vapor stretching across them. The Patriarch asked, "What do these omens portend?
He replied, "It cannot be known. The Patriarch said, "Fifty years after my passing, a calamity shall arise in the kingdom of Northern India."
"Ying is within your body; I am about to pass away. Now I entrust the Dharma-eye to you; guard and uphold it well. He then spoke a verse, saying:
"When the nature of mind is recognized, It may be called inconceivable. When it is clearly understood, there is nothing to be attained; When it is attained, one does not speak of knowing.
Having completed the transmission of the Dharma, he manifested eighteen transformations and returned to quiescence. After the cremation was finished, his relics were divided.
Each of them wished to erect a stupa for themselves. The Venerable One again appeared in mid-air and spoke a verse, saying:

"The one dharma encompasses all dharmas; all dharmas are subsumed within the one. My body is neither existent nor non-existent; how can one divide it among all these stupas? When the great assembly heard this verse, they no longer divided the remains.

They then constructed the stupa at the site of the *dhātu* (relics). (When karmic debts meet, incense forms into tassels; when the ancestral pulse flows secretly, extraordinary energies respond through to each other.)
The twenty-fourth patriarch, the Venerable Siṃhabhadra Bhikṣu, was a native of Central India.

He was of Brahmin lineage. Having attained the Dharma, he traveled abroad and arrived at the kingdom of Kaśmīra. There was a śramaṇa named Parika who had originally practiced the dhyāna-visualization of the Hīnayāna; he had five disciples, namely:

Śamatha-vipaśyanā (Meditative Concentration and Insight), Jñāna-darśana (Knowledge and Vision), Lakṣaṇa-grāha (Grasping at Characteristics), Lakṣaṇa-tyāga (Abandoning Characteristics), and Avāk (Silence). The Venerable One, by means of...
He refuted him with unimpeded eloquence and caused him to return to the correct path. Having gathered the fivefold assembly, his fame spread far and wide, and he then sought a Dharma heir.
He encountered an elder who brought forth his son and asked the Patriarch, "This boy’s name is Sthira;

from birth his left hand has been clenched into a fist, and though he is now twenty years old, it still cannot be opened. We pray that the Venerable One will reveal the cause of this in his past life. The Patriarch gazed upon him.
He immediately took it with his hand and said, "Return my pearl to me. The youth suddenly opened his hand and offered the pearl. The assembly was all struck with wonder.
The Patriarch said, "In a previous life, I was a monk named Vatsa. Once, when I went to a vegetarian feast by the Western Sea, I received this pearl as an offering and entrusted it to him.
That he now returns my pearl is but natural. The elder then caused him to leave the household life. This concludes the account of the Patriarch’s assembly.
The assembly of sages conferred upon him the full ordination. Because of these prior circumstances, he was named Vasiṣṭha. His master then said to him:
"My teacher had a secret prediction that you would encounter hardship before long. The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma shall now be entrusted to you;

you must protect it so that it may universally moisten all future generations. He spoke in verse: "When the true teaching of knowledge and vision is explained, Knowledge and vision are both the mind itself. At that time..."

The mind itself is knowing-seeing; knowing-seeing is right here and now. Having spoken this verse, the Patriarch secretly entrusted his saṃghāṭī robe to Sthiramati and sent him to another country to transform beings according to their capacities.
Having received these instructions, Sthiramati traveled directly to South India.
The Patriarch, deeming that the peril could not be evaded, remained alone in Kaśmīra. At that time, there were two non-Buddhist practitioners in that country, one named Māmuka...

There were many. The second was named Dūḍabha; he studied various magical arts and, wishing to conspire to cause a rebellion, deceitfully assumed the guise of a Śākya son and secretly entered the royal palace.
King Mīlinda then proceeded to destroy the teachings of the Śākyas. Grasping a sword, he went to where the Venerable One was and asked:
The King asked, "Have you attained the emptiness of the aggregates? The Patriarch replied, "I have already attained the emptiness of the aggregates.

The King asked, "Have you transcended birth and death? The Patriarch replied, "I have already transcended birth and death. The King said, "Since you have transcended birth and death, you may give me your head. The Patriarch replied, "This body is not mine; why should I be afraid of my head?
The King then brandished his blade and severed the Venerable One's head, whereupon white milk gushed forth several feet high from the Patriarch’s right shoulder.
His arm also fell to the ground, and he died seven days later. Prince Guangshou sighed, saying, "Why has my father brought this calamity upon himself?
He then gathered the assembly for repentance. At that time, there was a seer on Mount Baishe who deeply understood cause and effect.
He said, "In a previous life, both Siṃha and Rāhula were laymen. Because they envied the excellence of the Dharma, Siṃha secretly murdered Rāhula."

Now he repays them. The assembly subsequently erected a stupa for Zuobao Ti [based on the principle that] "the Way cannot be sought; its application is the manifestation of merit. (Though heads fall and arms are severed, karmic debts follow one another;
though heads fall before the blade, there is not the slightest difference between self and other.)
The twenty-fifth patriarch, Vasiṣṭha, was a native of Kaśmīra. His clan was Brahmin; his father was named Śāntacara and his mother was named Sukhāvatī.
Initially, his mother dreamed that she obtained a divine sword and subsequently conceived. Upon his birth, her left hand remained clenched in a fist.
He encountered the patriarch Siṃha, who transmitted the Dharma to him. Later, he traveled to Central India, where King Kaniṣka offered him ritual greetings and provisions.
There was a non-Buddhist teacher named Wuzun who was also honored and respected by the king. He then debated before the king, hoping to surpass his master and thereby enhance his own prestige.
He said to the Master, "I understand silent debate; it does not require spoken words. The Master asked, "Who shall determine victory and defeat?"
He said, "I do not contend for victory or defeat; I seek only the meaning. The Patriarch asked, "What do you take to be the meaning? He replied, "The absence of mind is the meaning.
The Patriarch said, "Since you have no mind, how can you attain the meaning? He replied, "When I speak of the absence of mind, it is the name, not the meaning.
The Patriarch said, "When you speak of the absence of mind, it is the name, not the meaning. When I speak of the absence of mind, it is the meaning, not the name."
The Master said, "That which is called 'meaning' is not the name. Who can distinguish meaning? The outsider said, "Your 'name' is not the meaning. What is this name?

The Master said, "It is for the sake of distinguishing what is not the meaning; thus, this name is a nameless name. The Master said, "Since the name is already not a name, the meaning is also not a meaning.
That which distinguishes is itself a name; what, then, would it distinguish? In this manner, they exchanged words fifty-nine times. The outsider was silenced.

The King and his ministers prostrated themselves in submission. At that moment, the Master suddenly turned northward, joined his palms, and sighed deeply, saying, "My teacher, the Venerable Siṃha, has encountered peril today;
this is truly lamentable. He then took leave of the king and traveled south, eventually entering into seclusion in the mountains and valleys of Southern India.
There, King Tiande welcomed him and offered him sustenance. The king’s second son, Arjuna, subsequently requested to leave the household life. The Master questioned him:
The Master asked, "If you wish to leave the household life, for what purpose do you intend to do so? Vimalamitra replied, "If I leave the household life, I shall not engage in those worldly affairs.
The Master asked, "What affairs will you not engage in? Vimalamitra replied, "I shall not engage in secular affairs. The Master asked, "Then for what purpose will you act?

Vimalamitra replied, "I shall act for the sake of the Buddha’s work. The Master said, "The Prince’s wisdom is as sublime as the heavens; surely it is that various sages have descended to manifest themselves. Thus he spoke.
He was ordained by Duzhu and served his master for six years. Later, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*). At the moment of the *karmavācanā*, the earth shook violently.

The master then bestowed upon him the verse of the transmission of the Dharma: "The Sage spoke of knowledge and vision; within the objective realm, there is neither right nor wrong. I have now realized true nature; there is neither the Path nor principle.
(The divine sword is inherently sharp; the jade ball is naturally lustrous. Their coming has its cause; the seal hangs from the elbow.)
The twenty-sixth patriarch, Venerable Rāhulamitra, was of the Kṣatriya caste and a prince of South India.
After attaining the Dharma, he traveled to East India, where its king, Drḍha, followed the non-Buddhist teacher, the Brahmin Dīrghanakha. When the Patriarch arrived, [the king]...
The king asked, "Master, for what purpose have you come? He replied, "I have come to deliver sentient beings. The king asked, "By what means do you deliver them?
He replied, "I deliver each according to their own kind. The Brahmin immediately conjured a great mountain above the Patriarch’s head, its momentum threatening to crush him down.

The Patriarch pointed at it, and the mountain suddenly shifted onto the heads of the assembly. Again, he pressed his hand against the ground; the earth shook, and five hundred heterodox practitioners were thrown into turmoil.

None of them were able to remain standing. The Brahmin was terrified and prostrated himself in repentance. The Patriarch again pressed down the earth, and it became still; he pointed at the mountain, and it vanished.
On another day, the King prepared a great vegetarian feast and gathered all the non-Buddhist practitioners, earnestly inviting the Patriarch to attend the assembly.

The Patriarch initially did not wish to go, but knowing that the site of the gathering was about to collapse, he went nonetheless. The King said, "Did you consent to come, Master? The Patriarch replied, "I am not one who partakes of offerings."
"I have come only to save you from death. This place has already become a dragon's lair; in a moment it will sink down. The King was terrified and, along with his retinue, fled to high ground.
Looking back, he saw that the site had already become a deep, swirling pool. The King’s reverence and faith increased further.
The Master expounded the Dharma for him, saying, "In this kingdom there shall be a sage who will succeed me in the Dharma. Previously, in eastern India, there had been the son of a Brahmin.

At the age of twenty, he lost both his parents while still young; their names and lineage were unknown. He sometimes called himself "Yingluo" (Adorned with Necklaces), and people consequently named him the "Boy Yingluo.
He wandered for alms through the streets and villages. If anyone asked, "Why do you walk so hurriedly? he would immediately reply, "Why do you walk so slowly?
If asked what his surname was, he would say, "It is the same as yours. No one could fathom him. One day, the King and his grandfather were traveling in the same carriage...
He emerged. [Da]yingluo bowed his head before him. The Patriarch asked, "Do you remember past events?
Yingluo replied, "I recall that in a previous kalpa, I lived together with you, Master. You expounded the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, while I expounded the profound Sūtras.
Today’s meeting is surely in accord with our past causes. The Patriarch looked at the King and said, "This is the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta; he shall appear hereafter."
There were two men: one was to convert South India, and the other’s karmic conditions lay in China. After nine years, he returned to this land. Based on his past causes, he was named Prajñātāra.
The verse of the transmission of the Dharma says: “The treasury of the true nature of the mind-ground has neither beginning nor end.

Through causes and conditions, it transforms sentient beings; through skillful means, it is called wisdom. [The commentary notes: The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) acted like a mountain, bringing calamity upon themselves. To cause them to return to the True Vehicle, [the Master] changed the curved into the straight.
To suddenly encounter an old friend (2 x 5 = 10).

The twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra, was a native of Eastern India. After attaining the Dharma, he went to Southern India, where the king, named Gandhāra, honored and made offerings to him with the utmost respect.
He surpassed all others in excellence, and the king further bestowed upon him a priceless jewel.
At that time, the king had three sons: Candravimala, Guṇavimala, and Bodhivimala. The youngest was a bodhisattva.
Desiring to test what each had attained, the grandfather took the pearls he had bestowed and asked the three princes:
"Is there anyone who can equal the perfect brilliance of these pearls? Candravimala and Guṇavimala both replied, "Among the seven treasures, these pearls—"
"Your Honor is indeed unsurpassed. Bodhi said: "This is a worldly treasure, yet it is not supreme. Among all treasures, the Dharma-treasure is supreme.
This is a worldly light, yet it is not supreme. Among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme."
This is a worldly light, yet it is not the supreme. Among all lights, the light of the mind is supreme.
This radiance of the jewel cannot illuminate itself; it must rely on the light of wisdom to discern it. Once it has been discerned, one then knows it to be a jewel.
"Thus, when the Master possesses the Way, his treasure immediately manifests; when sentient beings possess the Way, their mind-treasure is likewise so.
The Patriarch praised his discernment and wisdom, and then asked again: "Among all things, what thing is without form? He replied: "Among all things..."
Biqi Wuxiang was further asked: "Among all things, which is the highest? He replied: "Among all things, the human self (*ātman*) is the highest.
He was asked again: "Among all things, which is the greatest? He replied: "Among all things, the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is the greatest.

The Patriarch knew he was a vessel for the Dharma—transparent both in clarity and obscurity, his vision boundless and without spatial limits. One day, the King asked the various people: [...]* *Note: The original text fragment ends abruptly after "諸人" (various people).*

[The assembly] was reciting the sutras until the end. The Master asked, "Why do you not recite them? The Venerable One replied, "I, this poor monk, do not follow external conditions with my exhalation, nor do I dwell within the realms of the aggregates with my inhalation.
I am constantly reciting such a sutra as this—hundreds of thousands of millions of scrolls (from what source could one count so many scrolls?
Who knows this 'recitation of non-recitation'?). When King Xiangzhi grew weary of the world, the entire assembly wailed and fainted, yet Bodhidharma alone remained before the coffin."
He entered meditative absorption and emerged after seven days. He then followed his master to seek ordination. Once he had received full ordination (*upasampadā*), the master told him:
"The Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma (*saddharmacakṣus*) to Mahākāśyapa; in this manner it was passed down successively until it reached me.
I now entrust it to you. Listen to my verse: 'From the ground of the mind, all seeds arise; Through conditions, they further produce principles. When the fruit is full, Bodhi is perfected.'"

When the flowers bloomed, the world arose. Having transmitted the Dharma, he immediately rose from his seat, extended his left and right hands, and emitted twenty-seven rays of light from each, radiant with five colors.
He then leaped into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees.
He manifested fire to cremate himself; śarīras fell from the sky like rain. They were collected and used to construct a stupa. (Śrī-vigraha, Śrī-vigraha! You are the entrustment of the Dharma.
The turning of the sūtra does not rely on words and letters; the emission of light leaves no trace whatsoever.)
The First Patriarch of the Eastern Land, the Great Master Bodhidharma, was the third son of King Xiangzhi of South India.
His clan was Kṣatriya, and his original name was Bodhitāra. Later, he received the Dharma from the Venerable Prajñātāra.

The Venerable One said to him, "Regarding all dharmas, you have already attained thorough mastery (*pramāṇa*). Since *dharma* carries the meaning of 'thorough penetration,' I shall change your name accordingly.
The Patriarch respectfully received this instruction and served [the Venerable One] diligently for forty years.

Upon the Venerable One’s passing into *nirvāṇa*, he proceeded to propagate the teachings in his own country. At that time, there were two masters: the first named Buddhajīva and the second named Buddhatrāta. Together with...
The Master’s fellow student, Buddhabhadra, practiced the meditative contemplations of the Hīnayāna.

After Buddhabhadra encountered the Venerable Prajñāruci, he abandoned the Small Vehicle and turned toward the Great Vehicle, whereupon he and the Master worked together to transform beings; they were then known as the "Two Gateways of Ambrosia.

However, the latter was more successful and further divided his followers into six schools: first, the School of Manifest Characteristics (*sanimitta*); second, the School of Non-Manifest Characteristics (*animitta*); third, the School of Concentration...
The first was the School of Wisdom; the fourth, the School of Preceptual Practice; the fifth, the School of Non-Attainment; and the sixth, the School of Quiescence.

Each clung to their own understanding and separately expanded the source of their own conversion. The Patriarch sighed deeply and said, "If even one teacher has already fallen into the tracks of an ox, how much more so when they have fragmented [the teaching] into six schools?
If I do not eliminate this, it will remain forever entangled in false views. Having spoken, he subtly manifested his supernatural powers.
He went to the place of the Sarvāstivādins and asked, "What is called the 'true mark' (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas?
Among that assembly was a senior elder named Śarabha, who replied, "Among all marks, not mutually exchanging marks—this is called the true mark.
The Master said, "If all marks do not mutually exchange one another, this is called the true mark; by what means should this be determined? He replied, "Regarding all..."

"Among all characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there is in truth no fixedness. If characteristics were fixed, how could they be called 'real' (*bhūta*)? The Patriarch said: "The fact that all characteristics are not fixed is precisely what is called the 'characteristic of reality' (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
You yourself are currently not fixed; how then can you attain it? He replied: "When I say 'not fixed,' I am not speaking of characteristics.
When one speaks of characteristics, their meaning is likewise [not fixed]. The Patriarch said: "Your statement that [it] is 'not fixed' shall itself constitute the characteristic of reality."
"Because it is fixed and not fixed, it is not the true mark (dharmatā). He replied, "Since what is fixed is not fixed, it is not the true mark; this is because one knows that 'I' am not [existent].
The Master said, "If you are now unchanging, how can you be called the true mark? That which has already changed and passed away [is not the true mark]."
The meaning is likewise. He said, "If it were unchanging, it would have to exist; because it both exists and does not exist, the true mark (*dharmatā*) changes, and thus its meaning is established.
The Patriarch said, "The true mark is unchanging; if there is change, it is not the true mark. Within the realm of existence and non-existence, how can it be called the true mark?"

Śubhakarasiṃha knew in his heart that the Holy Master possessed profound and latent understanding. He immediately pointed his finger at empty space and said, "This is a conditioned phenomenon of the world, yet it can also be made empty.
Can this body of mine become like this? The Patriarch replied, "If you understand the true mark (*dharmatā*), you will see that there is no mark.
If you realize that there is no mark, then its form is likewise so. You must not lose yourself amidst form."
"The substance of form does not obstruct existence within the signless. When the assembly heard this, their minds became clear;
they paid homage with reverence and accepted it in faith. The Patriarch suddenly vanished his traces and went to the school of the Signless Sect.
A question was asked: "You say you realize the signless (*animitta*); by what means do you verify this? Among the assembly, Prajñātāra replied:
"I realize the signless because the mind does not manifest. The Patriarch said: "If your mind does not manifest, by what means do you realize it? He replied:
"I realize the signless because the mind neither grasps nor rejects. At the very moment of realization, there is no one who realizes. The Patriarch said: "Regarding all that exists..."

"There is nothing. The mind neither grasps nor rejects, and there is no one who 'should' [do so]. Since all clarity is absent, he said: 'Even when entering the Buddha-samādhi, there is still nothing to be attained;
how much more so for that which is signless—how could one wish to know it? The Patriarch said: 'If signs are not known, who speaks of existence or non-existence?
If there is still nothing to be attained, what do you call samādhi? He replied: 'I say that there is no realization; realization is the absence of anything to be realized. It is not...'"
"Because of samādhi, I speak of samādhi. The Patriarch said, "If it is not samādhi, what would you call it?

Since you have not yet realized it, what realization could there be apart from realization? When Pōluótí heard the Patriarch’s analysis, he immediately awakened to his original mind, prostrated in gratitude, and repented.
The Patriarch’s record says: "You shall attain the fruit; you will realize it before long. There is a demon in this land; you shall subdue him before long.
Having said this, he went to the abode of Dinghui Zong and asked, "In your study of concentration and wisdom, are they one or two?
Among the assembly was one named Póluántuó (Bhāradvāja), who replied, "This concentration and wisdom of mine are neither one nor two. The Patriarch said, "Since they are neither one nor two..."
"What do you mean by 'concentration and wisdom'? He replied, "In concentration there is no concentration; in wisdom there is no wisdom. One is not one, and two is not two.
The Patriarch said, "If being one is not one, and being two is not two, and they are neither concentration nor wisdom, then in terms of what can they be defined as concentration and wisdom?"

He said, "Neither one nor two; it is through concentration and wisdom that one can know. That which is neither concentration nor wisdom is likewise so. The Patriarch said, "Since wisdom is not concentration, how then does one know?
If they are neither one nor two, what is concentration and what is wisdom? When Vairocana heard this, his doubts were cleared away like ice melting.
He then went to the abode of the fourth master, Śīlabhadra, and asked, "What is called 'precept' (śīla)? How is it practiced?"
This is called "conduct. Regarding this conduct of precepts, is it one or two? Among that assembly, there was a worthy man who replied: "One is two, and two are one;
both are produced from that, and by relying on the teaching, they are untainted. This is called 'conduct of precepts. The Patriarch said:

"Your statement that one relies on the teaching implies there is still attachment. Since both 'one' and 'two' are destroyed, how can you say one relies on the teaching? These two are contradictory and do not reach [the truth]."

"Practice. When there is neither internal nor external clarity, what can be called precepts? He replied, "I have both internal and external. [The Master said,] "He has already attained full knowledge;

having achieved such penetration, this is itself the practice of precepts. If one speaks of contrariety, then all is both and all is not. When speech reaches purity, that is both precept and practice.
The Patriarch asked, "If all is both and all is not, how can you speak of purity? Since he has attained penetration, why discuss the 'internal'?"
Externally, when the worthy ones heard this, they immediately felt ashamed and submissive. They went to the place where Wude was the patriarch and asked, "You speak of 'no-attainment.

How can there be attainment through no-attainment? Since there is nothing attained, there is also no attainment of attainment. Among that assembly was one named Baojing, who replied, "When I speak of no-attainment, it is not the attainment of no-attainment;
rather, I am speaking of the attainment of attainment—no-attainment is itself attainment. The Patriarch said, "Attainment..."
"If it is not attained, then attainment itself is non-attainment. Since you speak of 'the attainment of attainment,' what is it that this 'attainment of attainment' attains?

The other replied, "Seeing attainment as non-attainment—that non-attainment is itself attainment. If one sees non-attainment, this is called the 'attainment of attainment. The Patriarch said, "If attainment is already non-attainment, then the 'attainment of attainment' is without attainment.
Since there is nothing to be attained, by what means could there be an 'attainment of attainment'? Upon hearing this, Baojing was suddenly freed from the net of doubt. He then... [continued].
At the Abode of Quiescence (Śāntivāda), someone asked: "What is meant by 'quiescence' (śānti)? Within this Dharma, what is it that becomes still and what is it that becomes quiescent?
A venerable one among the assembly replied: "This mind is unmoving; this is called 'quiescence. To be unstained by phenomena is called 'stillness' (śama). The Patriarch said:
"If the fundamental mind were not already quiescent, one would need to rely upon quiescence. Since it is quiescent from the very beginning, what use is there for further quiescence?"
The other said, "All dharmas are fundamentally empty; because they are empty of emptiness, they are called 'quiescence' within that emptiness of emptiness.
The Patriarch said, "If emptiness is already empty, so too are all dharmas. They are quiescent and signless; what is there to be stilled, and what is there to be made quiescent?

Upon hearing this instruction from the Master, the venerable one attained sudden and complete enlightenment. Subsequently, the six groups of followers all vowed to take refuge. From this, his transformation spread to the South.

His celestial reputation spread throughout the Five Indias, and for sixty years he delivered immeasurable multitudes. Later, he encountered King Vikṛtadarśana, who disparaged and reviled the Triple Gem, often saying:
"The ancestors of my lineage all believed in the Buddha-way, yet they fell into false views and their lifespans were not long."
Their reigns will also be short-lived. Moreover, since my very body is the Buddha, why seek it elsewhere?
All this is because those of excessive cleverness have fabricated such doctrines. Consequently, the elders within the kingdom who were honored by former kings have all been dismissed and degraded.
Foreseeing this, [the King] sighed at their meager virtue and wondered how he might save them. He then recalled the two leaders within the School of Formlessness (Mādhyamika).
One of the *pāṭhikas* had a karmic connection with the King and was about to realize its fruit.

As for the two who were superior in their respective schools, they were not lacking in extensive erudition, yet they lacked the necessary prior causes. At that time, the six disciples each thought to themselves, "The Buddha-Dharma faces a crisis;

why does our teacher remain so at ease? The Patriarch perceived the thoughts of the assembly from afar and immediately snapped his fingers in response. Hearing this, the six disciples said, "This is our teacher."

"The reputation of Bodhidharma has reached us; we ought to travel quickly to comply with your compassionate command. They immediately went to the Patriarch’s location, prostrated, and inquired after his well-being.
The Patriarch said, "A single leaf obscures the sky; who is able to trim and clear it away? Zongsheng replied, "Though I am shallow and humble, how could I dare shrink from this task?
The Patriarch said, "Though you possess eloquence and wisdom, your power of the Way is not yet complete. Zongsheng thought to himself, "Even if he possesses such merit and wisdom..."
"I am a king; I am a śramaṇa who has received the Buddha’s instructions. How could I be difficult to oppose? Having said this, he vanished and went to the king's location.
There, he extensively expounded the essentials of the Dharma, as well as matters concerning the suffering and happiness of the world, and the good and evil of humans and devas.

The king engaged him in a back-and-forth dialogue of inquiry and cross-examination, and there was nothing that did not accord with principle. The king asked, "As for the Dharma you now understand, where does its essence reside? Zongsheng replied:
"As a king governs and transforms his realm, he must accord with the Way. As for the Way you possess, O King, where does that Way lie?
The King replied, "The Way I possess is intended to eliminate heterodox teachings. As for the Dharma you possess, whom do you intend to subdue? Bodhidharma did not rise from his seat;

knowing intuitively that the Patriarch’s meaning was superior while his own fell short, he said to Prajñātāra, "The Patriarch’s meaning is superior. He has not received my instructions, yet he is secretly transforming the King."
"In a mere moment your reasoning will be exhausted; you must quickly save yourself. Pāṭaliputra respectfully received his master’s instructions.

Clouds arose from beneath his feet, and he arrived before the Great King, standing there in silence. At that time, the King was in the midst of questioning about the superiority of the doctrine when he suddenly saw Pāṭaliputra arrive riding upon the clouds.
Startled, he forgot his question and said, "One who travels through the air—is this right or wrong? Pāṭaliputra replied, "I..."
"I am neither heterodox nor orthodox; rather, I come to rectify both the orthodox and the heterodox. If Your Majesty’s mind is upright, I shall be neither heterodox nor orthodox.

Although the King was struck with wonder, his arrogance was still burning fiercely, and he immediately banished Zongsheng, ordering him to leave. Bōluótí said, "Since Your Majesty possesses the Way, why do you banish this śramaṇa?
Though I have no understanding, I pray that Your Majesty will put me a question. The King asked in anger, "Who is the Buddha? Tí—
[Zhaozhou] said, "To see one's nature is to be the Buddha. The King asked, "Does the Master see your nature? Dashi replied, "I see the Buddha-nature. The King asked, "Where does this nature reside?
Dashi replied, "The nature resides in its functioning. The King asked, "What is this functioning? I do not see it now.
Dashi replied, "It is functioning right now; it is simply that you, Your Majesty, do not see it. The King asked, "Is it present within me? Dashi replied, "If Your Majesty were to act..."
"There is nothing that is not used. If Your Majesty does not use it, its substance is likewise difficult to perceive. The King asked, "When it is being used, in how many places does it manifest?
Vimalakīrti replied, "If one observes when it manifests, there are eight instances. The King said, "When those eight manifestations occur, please explain them to me.
Vimalakīrti then spoke these verses: "In the womb, it is the body; In the world, it is the person. In the eye..."

It is said: seeing occurs in the eyes; hearing occurs in the ears; discerning fragrance occurs in the nose; discourse occurs in the mouth; grasping occurs in the hands; and running occurs in the feet.

These manifest everywhere, encompassing all within the sands of the Buddha-fields, yet when withdrawn, they are contained within a single minute speck of dust. One who recognizes this knows it to be the Buddha-nature.
Unaware of this, he called it his "spirit-soul. Upon hearing the verse, the King’s mind was immediately awakened;

he repented his past transgressions and inquired about the essentials of the Dharma, never wearying day or night until the end of the ninety-day retreat. At that time, Zongsheng, having been expelled, withdrew to hide in the deep mountains and thought to himself:
"I am now a hundred years old; for eighty years I committed wrongs, and only during the last twenty years have I returned to the Buddha-way. By nature..."
Although I am foolish and ignorant, my conduct has been free from blemish; yet I was unable to prevent this calamity, so what is life compared to death? He then threw himself off a cliff.
Suddenly, a divine being appeared and caught him with his hands, placing him upon a rock above. He was safe and sound, without injury.
Zongsheng said, "I am a śramaṇa by title and ought to be a guardian of the True Dharma. Because I could not suppress the king's transgressions, I have harmed my own body to reproach myself."
"What divine protection has aided you to such an extent? I pray that you will grant me a word. Thereupon, the divine being spoke this verse:
"The Master’s life shall reach one hundred years; at eighty, he committed a transgression. Because he drew near to the Most Honored One, he cultivated his practice and entered the Way."
Although he possessed a modicum of wisdom, he harbored much attachment to "self" and "other. Toward the various worthies he encountered, he never once gave rise to reverence or esteem.
For twenty years his meritorious practice, his mind remained unpacified; because of his cleverness and arrogance, he has come to this state.
"One who fails to show respect to a king shall experience such a retribution as this. From now on, do not be negligent; before long you shall achieve marvelous wisdom.
All the sages will keep you in their thoughts, and the Tathāgata likewise. When the eminent Zongsheng heard this verse, he was delighted and immediately sat in meditative seclusion upon the cliff.
At that time, the king again asked Pāṭali: "Worthy one, with such wisdom and eloquence, whom do you take as your teacher? Pāṭali replied:
The one from whom I received the precepts was the Tripitaka Master Uṣabha of the Bala Monastery, who served as my preceptor for receiving the teachings.
As for my teacher of the Way, he was the King’s uncle, Bodhidharma. When the King heard the Patriarch’s name, he was struck with awe and remained so for a long time.
[The King] said: "I, a humble and unworthy person, have shamefully succeeded to the royal throne. Yet I inclined toward the heterodox and turned my back on the orthodox, forgetting my honored uncle.

I hastily commanded my close ministers to specially invite you here. Your Reverence has now arrived with the envoys to perform repentance for my past transgressions. Upon hearing these admonitions, the King was moved.

He wept and apologized before his grandfather. Furthermore, an imperial decree was issued for Zongsheng to return to his own country. The high ministers reported, "Zongsheng was exiled and threw himself off a cliff; he is now dead.
The King said to his grandfather, "The death of Zongsheng is entirely my own fault. How can you be so great in compassion?"

He requested that [the master] be spared from this transgression. The Patriarch said, "Zongsheng is currently resting in seclusion among the crags. Simply dispatch a messenger to summon him, and he shall arrive immediately.
The King then sent a messenger into the mountains and indeed saw Zongsheng sitting upright in meditative stillness. Zongsheng received the summons.
He then said, "I am deeply ashamed of Your Majesty’s intention. This poor monk vows to dwell among the crags and springs. Furthermore, the King’s worthy virtues are as numerous as a forest;
Bodhidharma is Your Majesty’s uncle and the teacher of the Six Groups of Monks—a dragon-elephant within the *Prātimokṣa* Dharma.

I pray that Your Majesty will honor and revere these two sages, thereby blessing the imperial foundation. Before the messenger had returned with his report, the Patriarch said to the King, "Know that you have obtained the essence of the lineage."
"Will it be successful? The King replied, "I do not yet know. The Master said, "If one invitation does not suffice, a second command will surely bring him.
After a long while, the messenger returned; indeed, it was just as the Master had said. The Master then took his leave of the King, saying, "You should cultivate virtue well.

Before long, illness will arise, and I shall depart. Seven days passed, and the King fell ill. Court physicians examined and treated him, but the condition worsened without any improvement. The high nobles and close ministers—

Recalling his master’s previous prediction, he hurriedly dispatched a messenger to inform the Patriarch, saying: "The King is gravely ill, approaching the point of death. We pray that you, Uncle, will show compassion and come from afar to examine and save him.
The Patriarch immediately arrived to offer his condolences. At that time, Zongsheng received another summons from the King and thus departed from the mountain retreat.
Pralati also came to inquire after his illness. He asked the Patriarch, "What should be done to enable the King to escape this [suffering]?

The Patriarch immediately ordered the Crown Prince to act as regent, to pardon the King's offenses and bestow grace upon him, to reverently serve the Triple Gem, and further to perform repentance, vowing that the transgressions might be extinguished.

This was repeated three times, and the King’s illness abated. The Master then reflected that the conditions for China had ripened and that the time had come to travel there to transform beings; thus, he departed.
He entrusted his disciple Mi-mi-ta-lo (Maitrāyaṇīputra) to remain in India to transmit the Dharma. First, he took leave of the ancestral stūpa; next, he bid farewell to his fellow students;
finally, he went before the king, who consoled and exhorted him, saying: "You must diligently cultivate pure deeds and protect and uphold the Triple Gem.
My departure is not too late; I shall return within nine months. When the king heard the Master’s words, his tears flowed profusely, and he said: "What crime has this country committed?"
"What auspicious signs are there in that land? Since you, my nephew, have already established a karmic connection there, it is no longer where I shall dwell.

I only pray that you will not forget your ancestral homeland and return early once your mission is complete. The King then prepared a great ship, filled it with various treasures, and personally led his ministers and officials to escort him to the shore of the sea.
Zu then sailed across the vast ocean for three full cycles of winter and summer before reaching the South Sea. This was indeed the seventh year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty.
In the year of Gengzi, on the twenty-first day of the ninth month, Xiao Ang, the Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, received him with full official honors and submitted a memorial to Emperor Wu.
Upon reading the petition, the Emperor dispatched an envoy bearing an imperial decree to invite him. On the first day of the tenth month, he arrived at Jinling.
The Emperor asked, "Since my accession to the throne, the temples I have built, the scriptures I have transcribed, and the monks I have ordained are beyond counting."
"What merit is there? the Patriarch said, "There is no merit at all. The Emperor asked, "Why is there no merit?
The Patriarch replied, "This is merely a small fruit of the human and celestial realms, a cause of outflowing taints (*āsrava*). It follows the body like a shadow; though it exists, it is not real.
The Emperor asked, "What then is true merit? The Patriarch replied, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and tranquil. Such merit as this does not..."
Emperor Wu of Liang asked again, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths? The Patriarch replied, "Vast emptiness; there is no sage.
The Emperor asked, "Who is it that stands before me? The Patriarch said, "I do not know. The Emperor did not attain realization.

Knowing that his opportunity was not met, on the nineteenth day of that month, the Patriarch secretly returned north of the Yangtze River. On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month, he arrived in Luoyang and took up residence there.
At Shaolin Temple on Mount Song, he sat facing a wall, remaining silent throughout the day; no one could fathom him, and thus he was called the "Wall-Gazing Brahmin.
There was a monk named Shen Guang who had long resided in the region of Yi and Luo, where he had extensively studied various scriptures and was skilled at discoursing on profound principles.

He would often sigh and say, "The teachings of Confucius and Laozi, their rituals, arts, customs, and standards, as well as the texts of Zhuangzi and the *I Ching*, do not exhaust the wondrous principles.
I have recently heard that the Great Being Bodhidharma resides at Shaolin. Since this Supreme Person is not far away, I shall surely reach the profound realm.

He then went to visit the Patriarch to seek instruction. The Patriarch sat constantly with his face turned toward a wall, and no exhortations were heard. Huiguan reflected to himself, "Those of old who sought the Way..."

He pounded his bones to extract the marrow; he pierced his veins to relieve the hunger of others; he spread his hair to cover the mud; he threw himself from a cliff to feed a tiger. If the ancients were already like this, who am I to be otherwise?
When it snowed heavily, Dharma-śāma stood in attendance through the night. At dawn, the accumulated snow had risen above his knees, yet he stood with even greater reverence.
The Patriarch looked back at him and took pity on him. He asked, "You have stood in the snow for a long time; what do you seek?

Huiguan shed tears of sorrow and said, "I only pray that the Master, out of compassion, will open the gate of ambrosia to extensively deliver all classes of beings. The Patriarch replied, "The unsurpassed, wondrous Way of the Buddhas requires diligent effort over vast eons;
one must be able to perform what is difficult to perform and endure what is difficult to endure. How could it be attained through small virtue or small wisdom?"

With a frivolous and arrogant mind, yet hoping to attain the True Vehicle, you have merely exerted yourself in toil and hardship. Upon hearing this, Huiguang was inspired by the Patriarch’s admonition;
he secretly took a sharp blade and severed his own left arm before the Patriarch. The Patriarch, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, said:

"When the Buddhas first sought the Way, they forgot their very forms for the sake of the Dharma. Since you have now severed your arm before me, your seeking is indeed permissible. Thereupon, the Patriarch [accepted him].
His name was changed to Huìkě. Huìkě asked, "May I hear the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas? The Patriarch said, "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from another.
Huìkě said, "My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to grant me peace. The Patriarch said, "Bring forth your mind, and I will grant you peace.
After a long silence, Huìkě said, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unobtainable. The Patriarch said, "I have now granted you peace of mind."

Simply bring forth this robe along with my Dharma verses to manifest that my transformation is unimpeded.

Two hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, the robe shall cease to be transmitted, while the Dharma will encompass the entire realm of saṃsāra. There will be many who clarify the Way, but few who practice it;

The Second Patriarch, Great Master Huike, was a native of Wulao and the son of Lady Ji.
His father, JI, having long prayed for an heir without success, one night beheld a wondrous light illuminating the chamber; his mother subsequently conceived. Thus, he was named Guang at birth.

In his youth, he was transcendent, having read extensively through the archives of all learning and being particularly adept at discussing Laozi and Zhuangzi. Later, upon examining the Buddha-vehicle, he ultimately abandoned all [worldly studies] behind him.

He left the household life under the guidance of Master Baojing and studied the doctrines of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna extensively. At the age of thirty-three, he returned to Mount Xiangshan, where he remained in constant seated meditation.
After another eight years, while in a state of profound silence, he suddenly beheld a divine being who said to him, "You are about to receive the fruit [of enlightenment];

However, the spirit commanded him to go to Runan. There, at Shaolin, was the Great Being Bodhidharma; he would surely be your teacher. The Patriarch then proceeded to Mount Shaoshi.

after transmitting the Dharma, he lived in seclusion at Mount Wangong in Shu. He traveled between Mount Sikong in Taihu County and other locations.

During the persecution of the Dharma under the Later Zhou dynasty, the Patriarch deeply concealed his identity and had no fixed abode for more than ten years, such that no one could recognize him. This continued until the tenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.

Two years later, there was a novice named Daoxin, fourteen years of age, who came to pay his respects to the Patriarch and said, "I pray that the Master will show compassion and grant me the Dharma-gate of liberation.

At these words, Daoxin attained great enlightenment. He served the Patriarch for nine years, after which he received full ordination in Jizhou and remained in attendance.

From birth he was extraordinary; from childhood he admired the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and his mastery of the various gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) appeared as if it were the result of past habituation.

Having inherited the patriarchal tradition, he concentrated his mind without sleep; for sixty years his side did not touch his mat. This was during the thirteenth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty.

Day and night without ceasing, eight months passed. The Patriarch, knowing that the time for the transmission had arrived, addressed the assembly, saying:

"The True Dharma is difficult to understand; it must not be merely memorized as my words. You must take this as your own responsibility. Each of you should independently compose a verse according to your own understanding.

If the meaning of your words accords with my intent, then both the robe and the Dharma shall be transmitted to you. At that time, there were more than seven hundred monks in the assembly, including the Elder Shenxiu.

This person’s learning was thorough in both the inner and outer teachings, and he was revered by all. Everyone praised him, saying, "Were it not for one as venerable and eminent as this, who would dare to hold such a position?
Shenxiu secretly heard these public accolades and, without further reflection, inscribed a verse upon a corridor wall, which said:

"The body is the Bodhi tree; The mind is like a stand for a bright mirror. At all times diligently wipe and polish it, So that no dust or grime may gather. —From the *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch* (Zu)

While walking in meditation, he suddenly saw this verse. Knowing it was composed by Shenxiu, he praised it, saying, "If future generations practice according to this, they too shall attain the supreme fruit.
While Lu was at the mill, he suddenly heard the verse being recited and asked his fellow students, "What verses are these?
His fellow students replied, "You do not know that the Master is seeking a successor and has ordered each of you to compose a verse on the mind. This...
The Abbot deeply praised what the Elder Xiu had described, saying, "He will surely be entrusted with the Dharma and the robe.
Lu asked, "What was his verse? His fellow students recited it for him. After a long while, Lu said, "It is beautiful, but it is not yet complete.
His fellow students rebuked him, saying, "How can a mediocre person like you know this? Do not utter such mad words. Lu replied, "Do you not believe me? I pray—"
He composed a verse in response to it. His fellow student did not answer, but merely looked at him and smiled. That night, Lu secretly told a young boy to lead him to the corridor.
There, Lu personally held a candle and invited Zhang Riyong, the Regional Inspector, and Yu Xiuzhi to stand beside the verse.

He wrote a verse, saying: "Bodhi originally has no tree; The bright mirror is also not a stand. Fundamentally there is not a single thing— Where, then, could dust and grime settle? Later, the Patriarch saw this verse and said, "Who wrote this? They have not yet seen their nature. When the assembly heard the Patriarch’s words, they paid it no further heed. That night, the Patriarch went secretly to the rice-hulling room and asked, "Is the rice white yet? Huiming replied, "It is white. The Patriarch said, "Bring me some. Huiming took a scoop and gave it to him. The Patriarch tasted it and said, "It is not yet white. Huiming returned and pounded again. The Patriarch tasted it once more and said, "Now it is white. Huiming then bowed. The Patriarch said, "Your mind is already white; you need only grind away the husks. Huiming then composed another verse, saying: "Originally there was nothing at all; How could there be a tree of Bodhi? Since the bright mirror is not a stand, Where could dust and grime settle? Upon seeing this verse, the Patriarch said, "This one has indeed seen their nature. He then transmitted the Dharma to him and had him succeed to the patriarchal seat. Thus, Huiming became the Third Patriarch. He resided at Caoqi for thirty years and passed away in the second year of the Yongchun era (676 CE). His remains were enshrined in a stupa named "Dongshan" (East Mountain). His dharma heirs numbered one hundred and thirty-nine. Among them, the most prominent were Nanyue Huairang and Qingyuan Xingsi. Their descendants flourished and spread throughout the world. This concludes the account of the Third Patriarch, Huiming. It is said that he was a man from Shaozhou. His secular surname was Lu. His father was a high official who served as the Governor of Shaozhou. During his youth, he studied the Confucian classics. Later, he encountered a monk who taught him the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. He then abandoned his family and entered the mountains to practice austerities. He lived in seclusion for many years, eventually encountering the Second Patriarch, who transmitted the Dharma to him. After receiving the transmission, he traveled to various places to propagate the teaching. Eventually, he settled at Caoqi, where he remained for thirty years. He passed away in the second year of the Yongchun era. His remains were enshrined in a stupa named "Dongshan. His dharma heirs numbered one hundred and thirty-nine. Among them, the most prominent were Nanyue Huairang and Qingyuan Xingsi. Their descendants flourished and spread throughout the world. This concludes the account of the Third Patriarch, Huiming.
