He replied, "It is Bai. There has not yet been a sieve. The Patriarch struck the mortar three times with his staff; Lu immediately beat the drum three times and entered the room.
The Patriarch told him, "The Buddhas appear in the world for one great purpose: to guide beings according to their varying capacities."
Consequently, there arose the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the three vehicles (*triyāna*), and the doctrines of sudden and gradual enlightenment as the gateways of teaching.

Nevertheless, the unsurpassed, subtle, secret, perfectly luminous, and true *dharmaparyāya*—the Eye-Treasury of the True Dharma (*saddharmapuṭa*)—was entrusted to the preeminent Venerable Mahākāśyapa.
It was transmitted in succession through twenty-eight generations until it reached Bodhidharma, who arrived here in this land and found the Great Master Huike to inherit it.
Up until now, I have used the Dharma-treasure and the robe transmitted to me to entrust to you. Protect them well yourself; do not allow them to be severed. Listen to my verse:
"When sentient beings come to sow seeds, The fruit arises from the ground. Since insentient things have no seeds, That which lacks nature has no arising.
Having received [the transmission], Lu knelt and asked: "Since the Dharma-methods have already been received, to whom shall the robe be entrusted? The Patriarch said: [To Xingtao].
He said: "In the past, when Bodhidharma first arrived, people did not yet believe him; therefore, he transmitted the robe to manifest his attainment of the Dharma.

Now that faith has matured, the robe is merely a source of contention. It shall end with you; it will no longer be transmitted. (When he came, there was an agreement: the place of birth is difficult to trace.
When the fruit of Huangmei ripens, let the wind blow it away. One scroll of the Diamond Sutra constitutes a formal proclamation.)
The Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng, was surnamed Lu. His father was named Xingtao and his mother, Lady Li, experienced a miraculous dream.
Upon awakening, a wondrous fragrance filled the room, and she subsequently conceived. Six years later, he was born; at that time, rays of light soared into the sky.
At dawn, a monk came and said to the Patriarch’s father, "This son should be named Huineng. The father asked, "What does this mean? The monk replied, "Hui means wisdom."
He bestowed the Dharma as a means of relief for sentient beings. One capable of this can perform the work of a Buddha. Having finished speaking, he was gone, no one knowing where he had gone.
The Patriarch did not drink his mother’s breast milk; when night fell, a divine being poured nectar upon him. At the age of three, his father passed away and his mother became a widow.
Their household was in extreme poverty; from a young age, he gathered firewood and sold it to support his mother. One day, while carrying firewood through the marketplace, he heard a guest reading.

Upon reaching the passage in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling anywhere," he attained a profound realization. He asked a traveler, "What teaching is this?
The traveler replied, "This is the *Vajracchedikā*. The Fifth Patriarch, Master Ren of Dongshan at Huangmei, constantly teaches people to recite this sūtra.
Upon hearing these words, he was suddenly moved and resolved to leave home to seek the Dharma; he then begged for it from the traveler.

His mother had prepared a year’s worth of provisions for him, so he took his leave of her and traveled directly to Shaozhou. There he met the man of noble conduct Liu Zhilüe and formed a friendship with him.
A nun named Wujinzang was Zhilüe’s paternal aunt; she had been reading the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and when the Master briefly listened to it, he immediately explained its meaning to her.
The nun then took up the scroll and asked about the characters, to which the Patriarch replied, "I do not recognize the characters."

He then inquired about the meaning [of the text]. The nun said, "I do not even recognize the characters; how could I possibly comprehend their meaning? The Master said, "The wondrous principle of the Buddhas has nothing to do with written words.
The nun was struck with wonder and amazement, and she informed the elders of her village, requesting that he reside at Baolin Monastery.

Although the monastery had been in ruins for a long time, the fourfold assembly labored to restore it, gathering there morning and evening until it was suddenly transformed into a magnificent temple complex. The Master said, "I seek the Great Dharma."
"What is the point of staying here? he said, and so he abandoned it. He traveled to Huangmei and paid his respects to the Fifth Patriarch. At the third watch, he entered the inner chamber.
The Fifth Patriarch again questioned him regarding his initial realization concerning the words, "Give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere. Upon hearing these words, he attained great enlightenment.
He then addressed the Fifth Patriarch, saying, "All dharmas do not depart from self-nature. Who would have expected that self-nature is fundamentally pure by its very nature?"
"How unexpected that the self-nature is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished! How unexpected that the self-nature is fundamentally and spontaneously complete!

How unexpected that the self-nature is fundamentally unmoving! How unexpected that the self-nature can give rise to the myriad dharmas! The Fifth Patriarch, knowing that [Huineng] had awakened to his original nature, said to him:
"If you do not recognize your own mind, studying the Dharma is of no benefit. If you recognize your own mind and see your own original nature, you are immediately a celestial being."

He took refuge in the Buddha and subsequently received the transmission of the robe and the Dharma. The Fifth Patriarch escorted him as far as the Jiuyang Post Station and ordered him to board the boat.

As Huineng took up the oars, the Fifth Patriarch said, "It is I who should have delivered you. Huineng replied, "When one is deluded, the teacher delivers; when one is awakened, one delivers oneself."

Although the name "deliverance" (tú) is one, its applications differ. Since you have been able to receive the transmission of the Dharma from your teacher and have now attained enlightenment, you ought to deliver yourself by means of your own nature.

The Fifth Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is. The Buddha-dharma shall be widely propagated through you. (The Sixth Patriarch was no hero of that time; he asked another to write on the wall for him and then plastered over it himself.

Though there was clearly a verse stating "there is nothing," he instead accepted a single alms bowl from the other house. After the Patriarch had paid his respects and bid farewell, he traveled south for two months until he reached...
At Mount Dayu, the monk Huiming, formerly a general, arrived with several hundred men intending to seize the robe and bowl.
The Patriarch cast the robe and bowl onto a rock and said, "This robe represents my faith; can it be taken by force? When Huiming lifted the robe and bowl, he was unable to move them.
He then said, "I have come for the sake of the Dharma; I have not come for the sake of robes.
The Patriarch said, "Since you have come for the sake of the Dharma, you should set aside all external conditions and do not give rise to a single thought. I shall speak for you.

After a long silence, the Patriarch said, "At this very moment, when you are neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil—what is that which is the original face of Master Ming? At these words, Huiming attained great awakening.
Wu (Huineng) asked again, "Apart from these secret words and secret meanings you have just provided, is there still another secret intent?
The Patriarch said, "That which I have spoken to you is not secret. If you turn back and reflect upon yourself, the secret is right there with you.

Huiming said, "Although Huiming was at Huangmei, I truly did not realize my own true face. Now that I have received your instruction, it is like a person drinking water—the coolness [is known by oneself]."
Daran himself was aware of this. Thereafter, he remained hidden among the Huinji and Sihui regions, mingling within a band of hunters for sixteen years.
On the eighth day of the first month of the first year of the Yifeng era, he suddenly felt that the time had come to preach the Dharma;
he accordingly traveled to Faxing Monastery in Guangzhou, where he encountered Master Yinzong lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. He stayed overnight in the corridors of the monastery. At dusk, he...
The wind blew the banners on the temple spires. Hearing two monks debating, one said, "The banner moves," and the other said, "The wind moves.

As they argued back and forth without end, the Patriarch said, "It is not the wind that moves; it is not the banner that moves. It is your own mind that moves. The entire assembly was struck with awe. (It is neither the banner nor the wind;

here the patch-robed monk establishes the transmission. Crossing the river with a raft is an ordinary matter; when the southern mountain burns charcoal, the northern mountain turns red. On the fifteenth day of the first month, [he] sealed [it].
Zonghui gathered various eminent virtuous masters and had his head shaved for the sake of the Patriarch on the eighth day of the second month.

On that same day, he received the full ordination from Vinaya Master Zhiguang at Faxing Temple. That ordination platform was originally established by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra during the Song dynasty.
The *Sanzang ji* states: "In the future, there shall be a flesh-body Bodhisattva who will receive the precepts upon this altar.
Furthermore, at the end of the Liang dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha personally planted two Bodhi trees beside the altar and said to the assembly:
"One hundred and twenty years hence, a great Mahāsattva shall appear beneath these trees to expound the Unsurpassed Vehicle and deliver immeasurable multitudes. This is the Patriarch.
Having received the precepts, he opened the Dharma gate of the Eastern Mountain beneath this tree, as if fulfilling a long-standing covenant.

In the first year of the Zhongzong era, the Emperor dispatched the inner attendant Xue Jian to deliver an imperial decree inviting him to court. The Patriarch submitted a memorial declining on the grounds of illness, wishing to spend his final years among the forest slopes.
Xue Jian said, "The Chan masters of the capital all say that if one wishes to realize the Way, one must practice seated meditation and cultivate samādhi. I do not know whether the Master..."
"What do you say? The Patriarch replied, "The Way is realized through the mind; how could it depend on sitting? A sutra says:
'If one perceives the Tathāgata as either sitting or lying down, this is practicing a deviant path. Why? Because there is nowhere from which he comes, nor anywhere to which he goes.

If there is neither arising nor ceasing, this is the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata. That all phenomena are empty and quiescent—this is the pure sitting of the Tathāgata. Ultimately, there is nothing..."
[The Master] testified, "How much more so for sitting? He asked about the essentials of the mind. The Patriarch said: "The Way has neither light nor darkness;

light and darkness are merely the meaning of alternation. Light and darkness are inexhaustible, yet they are also exhaustible; their names are established in mutual dependence. As the Sūtra says: "The Dharma has no peer."
Because they do not exist in mutual dependence. Jian said, "Light is used as a metaphor for wisdom; darkness is illustrated by means of afflictions.
The Patriarch said, "Afflictions are themselves bodhi; they are neither two nor distinct. If one uses wisdom to illuminate afflictions, this is the limited view of the Two Vehicles."
Those of great wisdom and superior faculties are not like this at all. When asked specifically about the Mahāyāna, the Patriarch said: "Luminosity and ignorance are non-dual in their nature.
This non-dual nature is the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). As for the true nature: it does not diminish when among the foolish and ignorant;

it does not increase when among the worthy and sages; it is not disturbed while abiding in afflictions; it is not quiescent while dwelling in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); it is neither severed nor..."
It is eternal. It neither comes nor goes; it is not in between, nor within or without. It is neither born nor extinguished;
its nature and characteristics are suchness (*tathatā*). Constantly abiding and never shifting—this is called the Way. Jian asked: "The Master speaks of 'neither born nor extinguished.

How does this differ from the non-Buddhists? The Patriarch said: "What the non-Buddhists call 'neither born nor extinguished' involves using extinction to stop birth, and using birth to manifest extinction."
What I call non-arising and non-ceasing is that which is fundamentally unborn and, even now, unceasing.

If you wish to know the essential point of the mind, simply do not engage in any deliberation regarding good or evil; you will naturally enter the essence of the pure mind, which is profoundly still and eternally tranquil, its wondrous functions as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
Jianmeng was suddenly and greatly enlightened. When the Patriarch arrived at Baolin Temple in Caoxi, he beheld...
The hall was cramped and narrow. He went to see his fellow villager Chen Ya-xian and said, "I, an old monk, wish to beg for a space the size of a single *tānana* (seating mat) from you.
Ya-xian agreed. The Patriarch spread out his seating mat, which covered the four borders of Caoxi. (That the mat was so wide while the four borders were so contracted is a matter of spiritual power;
it is not merely a lack of spiritual power. One day, the Patriarch said to the assembly, "All of you, your own minds are the Buddha. Do not seek further..."
Doubt and hesitation. Though there is not a single external thing, one is able to establish all things; it is all the original mind that gives rise to the myriad dharmas.
If you wish to accomplish various kinds of wisdom, you must attain the Samādhi of One Mark and the Samādhi of One Practice, and remain non-abiding with respect to all phenomena.
Within those signs, one does not give rise to hatred or love; there is neither grasping nor rejecting. One does not dwell upon matters such as benefit or failure, success or ruin.
One is at ease, tranquil, empty, harmonious, and detached. This is called the Samādhi of the Single Sign.

If, in all places—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—one maintains a pure and direct mind, remaining unmoved within the site of enlightenment, one directly accomplishes the Pure Land. This is called the Samādhi of the Single Practice. If...
A person who possesses two or three samādhis is like the earth with seeds, capable of containing and nurturing them. Chan Master Shenxiu was surnamed Li;
he was a native of Weishi in Bianzhou. In his youth, he read widely through the classics and histories. At the end of the Sui dynasty, he left the household life and took Hongren as his teacher.
Hongren said to Xiù, "I have ordained many people, but none has surpassed you in terms of intuitive liberation and perfect illumination."—Hongren.
He passed away in the fifth year of the Xianheng era. Shenxiu then went to Jingzhou and resided at Mount Dangyang. Empress Wu Zetian, having heard of his reputation, summoned him to the capital.

She had him carried to the palace on a sedan chair and personally performed the ritual of prostration before him. By imperial decree, she established Duzhi Monastery on Mount Dangyang to commemorate his virtue.
At that time, from princes and dukes down to commoners and citizens, all came to pay their respects; they would bow and prostrate themselves upon merely seeing his dust. — Emperor Zhongzong.

Upon his accession to the throne, [the Emperor] showed him even greater reverence and esteem. Xiu and Huineng were fellow students under Hongren. After Hongren’s death, Huineng went to Guangguo Temple in Shaoguo.
Each part of the world transmitted their respective teachings; thus, Shenxiu was called the Northern School and Huineng the Southern School (The peach blossoms are white, the plum blossoms are red;
the sun rises in the west and sets in the east). Master Nanyue Huairang paid homage to the Patriarch, who asked: "From where have you come?"
He came forward and said, "From Mount Song. The Patriarch asked, "What kind of thing comes like this? He replied, "If one tries to describe it as a thing, it is not quite right.
The Patriarch asked, "Is there still need for cultivation and realization? He replied, "Cultivation and realization are not absent, yet it cannot be defiled. The Patriarch said:
This very state is undefiled; it is that which all Buddhas protect and keep in mind. Since you are thus, I am also thus. The Indian Prajñātāra prophesied at your feet:
"A colt shall emerge who will trample the people of the world to death. This must reside within your own person.
Zen Master Xingxi of Qingyuan went to visit the Patriarch and asked: "What should I devote myself to? Immediately, he did not fall [into conceptualization].
Regarding "ranks": The Patriarch asked, "What have you practiced? He replied, "I do not even practice the Noble Truths. The Patriarch asked, "In what rank do you fall?
He replied, "Since I do not even practice the Noble Truths, what rank could there be? The Patriarch held him in high esteem.
At that time, there were thirty people who attained the Dharma, but Yuezhou Yuan alone was the foremost at Caoxi. Chan Master Xuanjue of Yongjia studied the scriptures in his youth.
The Treatise: Having mastered the Dharma-gate of the Tiantai *Zhiguan* and read the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, he clarified the ground of the mind.
Later, encouraged by Chan Master Zuo Xi Lang, he traveled with Chan Master Yang Ce to Caoxi.

Upon first arriving, he shook his staff, circumambulated three times, and stood upright. The Patriarch said, "A śramaṇa possesses three thousand dignified manners and eighty thousand subtle practices."
"Virtuous One, from where have you come? You have given rise to great conceit. The Master said, "Matters of birth and death are great; impermanence is swift.

The Patriarch said, "Why do you not realize non-arising? Why do you not understand that there is no swiftness? The Master said, "Realization itself is non-arising; understanding is fundamentally without swiftness."
The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is. At that time, the entire assembly was not without astonishment. Huairang then assumed his full ceremonial demeanor and paid his respects;
after a short while, he took his leave. The Patriarch said, "Are you returning too soon? Stay for one night. Consequently, he was called "One-Night Huairang" (Yi-xiu Jue).
The monk Zhìtōng had read the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* more than a thousand times, yet he could not comprehend the Three Bodies and Four Wisdoms. He prostrated before the Patriarch to seek an explanation.
The Patriarch said: "As for the Three Bodies: the Pure Dharma Body is your nature; the Perfectly Full Reward Body is your wisdom;
and the thousands of billions of Transformation Bodies are your practice. If you were to speak of the Three Bodies apart from your original nature, then they would be nothing but empty names."
This is called having a body but lacking wisdom. If one awakens to the fact that the three bodies have no inherent nature, this is then called the Bodhi of the four wisdoms.

Listen to my verse: The three bodies are inherently complete; Their manifestation gives rise to the four wisdoms. Without departing from the conditions of seeing and hearing, One transcends and ascends to the stage of Buddhahood.
I now speak for you; believe this with clarity, And you shall forever be free from delusion. Do not follow those who run in pursuit, Spending their whole days...

He spoke of Bodhi. Tong said, "I would like to hear the meaning of the four wisdoms. The Patriarch said, "Since you have already understood the three bodies, you must clearly comprehend the four wisdoms;
why do you ask again? If one were to speak of the four wisdoms apart from the three bodies, this would be called 'having wisdom but no body';
such wisdom would, in turn, become non-wisdom. He then spoke a verse: "The nature of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure and clear."

The Wisdom of Equality has no affliction in the mind; the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees that there is no effort. The Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks is identical to the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.
Regarding the transformation of the fruits and causes of the five, eight, six, and seven [consciousnesses]: they are merely conventional designations and lack any real nature.

If one leaves no lingering attachment at the point of transformation, then amidst the profusion of activity, one dwells eternally in *yoga-samādhi*. (Transforming the first five consciousnesses results in the Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks; transforming the sixth consciousness results in the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation; transforming the seventh consciousness...)

The eighth consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Equality; the seventh and sixth consciousnesses are transformed during the causal stage, while the fifth and eighth are transformed upon the attainment of the fruit—this is called "transformation" (though their substance does not transform).
A monk asked, "Who can attain the essential meaning of Huangmei? The Patriarch said, "One who understands the Buddha-dharma. The monk asked, "Does the Master yourself attain it?
The Patriarch replied, "I do not understand the Buddha-dharma. On the eighth day of the seventh month, he said to his disciples, "I wish to return to Xinzhou."

The eleventh patriarch, Chan Master Chiming (Buchu Yuan) of Shishuang in Tanzhou, was a successor of Fenyang.
He was the son of the Li family of Qingxiang in Quanzhou. In his youth, he was a scholar. At the age of twenty-two, he received full ordination at Yijing Temple on Mount Xiang south of the city.
His mother was a woman of virtuous conduct and encouraged him to travel to study under various masters. The Master had joined eyebrows and prominent eyes; he was tall and robust in stature.
However, he suddenly disregarded the rules of the monastic code, and wherever he went, he was rebuked by senior elders as being too young for the monastic community (*saṅgha*).

The Master laughed with a voice like a crashing cliff, saying, "The treading of dragons and elephants is not something a donkey can endure. He once carried a chest of miscellaneous relics in a bag, slung over his shoulder on a bamboo staff.

While traveling between the regions of Xiang and Mian, he joined forces with Shou to visit Zhiguquan. Together they traveled to the capital, where they heard that Chan Master Fenyang Zhao’s reputation for the Way was preeminent in the world.
Resolving to rely upon him personally, they arrived just as the imperial court was mobilizing to punish the region of Hedong.
Lü and Ze both stationed heavy troops there, and many urged him not to proceed. The Master paid no heed;

he crossed the Great River, ascended Mount Taihang, changed his clothes to resemble those of a servant, and concealed his identity within a fire-guard unit. Sleeping in the open and lodging in the grass, he reached Longzhou and went to see Fenyang.
Duke Zhao admired him, yet for two years he did not permit him to enter his inner quarters. The Master visited Duke Zhao, who perceived his resolve and was certain that—
He scolded and commanded those under his authority, or slandered and reviled people in all directions; whatever instructions he gave were all vulgar matters of worldly custom.
One night, [a disciple] complained, saying: "Since arriving at this Dharma assembly two summers ago, I have received no guidance; I have only increased my worldly afflictions."
"Reflecting on how the years and months have slipped by in an instant, my own practice remains unclarified; I have lost the benefit of leaving the household life.

Before he had finished speaking, Duke Zhao stared at him intently and scolded, "This evil teacher of the Dharma dares to deceive and exploit me! In a rage, he raised his staff to drive him away. The Master prepared to intervene in his defense.
Zhao Gong covered his mouth. Shida awakened greatly and said, "Now I know that Linji’s Way transcends ordinary circumstances.
He served him for seven years and then took his leave, following Chan Master Tangming Song. Because his mother was elderly, he returned south and followed Chan Master Dongshan Cong as his head seat.
Huang Zongdan, the Governor of Yichun, invited him to take charge at Nanuan; he resided there for three years before departing.
He went to pay his respects to Chan Master Shen Dingyin. Master Ding was a senior disciple of Shou Shan;

his reputation was preeminent at the time, and among the monastics, none dared to enter his gate unless they were of extraordinary refinement and talent. The Master had not cut his hair and wore tattered clothes while speaking with a Chu accent.

When he presented himself, calling himself a "Dharma nephew," the entire assembly laughed loudly. Master Ding sent a young attendant to ask, "Whose successor is this elder? The Master looked up at the roof.
[The Master] said, "I have personally seen [Zhao] Fenyang come; when I went out with my staff, he looked back at me with joy.
I asked him, 'Is there a lion of the West River in Fenzhou? The Master pointed behind him and cried out, 'The house is collapsing! The boy fled backward.
As Zhao Ding turned around to look back, the Master was sitting on the ground, having taken off one of his sandals to show him. Old Yìn forgot what he had asked and lost sight of the Master."
The Master rose slowly, adjusted his robes, and as he walked away, he said, "To see a person is not as good as hearing of their reputation.

He then departed. Baizhang sent someone to pursue him, but it was to no avail. He sighed and said, "Fenyang has such a son! From that time on, the Master’s reputation grew weighty within the monastic community.

When Daowu’s seat became vacant, Baizhang personally recommended the Master to preside over it. His administration of the Dharma was strict and orderly; he would risk his own life for the sake of the teaching.
The Way is where all gathers. Next, he resided at Shishuang and greatly propagated the Way of Linji.
Addressing the assembly, he struck the meditation seat once with his staff and said, "Does the great assembly understand? Have you not heard it said: 'One blow causes all knowledge to be forgotten;
no further cultivation or refinement is required'? Those who have attained the Way in various quarters all say this is the highest capacity. Xiangyan realized it in this very way."
"You have clearly awakened to the Tathāgata-dhyāna, but you have not even dreamed of the Patriarchal-dhyāna. Now tell me, what excellence does the Patriarchal-dhyāna possess?

All phenomena are fundamentally at rest; it is only people who create their own clamor. Therefore, while I dwell at Fuyan, I see only this:"
In the realm of Fuyan, one rises late and sleeps early. Sometimes clouds arise from the azure crags; sometimes the moon sets behind the cold pool.
The kalavinka birds fly and sing before the Prajñā Terrace; the śāla flowers scatter their fragrance beside Mount Zhurong.
Grasping a lean bamboo staff, I sit upon the Paṇḍaka Rock, occasionally discussing the profound and subtle with the monks of the Five Lakes. With hair like ash and face like dust, I dwell in Xing.
Transformation. One sees only the house style of Xinghua: welcoming and seeing off guests; the gate connects with the city, where carriages and horses are packed together.
There is the singing of fishermen by the Xiao and Xiang rivers and the cries of monkeys at Mount Lu. The sounds of stringed and bamboo instruments and songs enter the ears at all times.

Furthermore, he daily discusses Chan and the Way with eminent men from the four seas, forgetting the passage of years and months. Now tell me: dwelling in deep mountains or residing in the city walls—does one have any difference?

Throughout his life, the Master practiced the mind of the non-obstruction of all phenomena (*sarva-vastu-asaṅga*), which neither ordinary beings nor sages could fathom. He would sit in serene meditation within his quarters.

He placed his sword across the top of a water basin and set out a straw sandal beside it, instructing those who came to seek instruction to offer a response as a means to test their spiritual resonance with the Dharma.
He entered nirvana on the fifth day of the first month in the Gengchen year of the Kangding era (1060). His stupa was erected at Shishuang. Seventeen people succeeded him in the Dharma.

(Fenyang possessed the "Great Function of the Total Mechanism," which enabled Ciming to cast off the cage beneath his teacher's influence; Shending possessed the "eye that kills with bare hands" and surpassed all others. Truly, he was a peerless leader in the Great Way, carefree and unimpeded.)
[He] simply practiced in this manner).
The twelfth [patriarch], Chan Master Fănghuì of Yángqí, was a successor of Címíng. He was the son of the Lěng family in Yíchūn, Yuánzhōu.

From his youth, he was alert and quick-witted; he did not concern himself with brush or inkstone. Upon leaving the household life, whenever he read the scriptures, he immediately attained spiritual realization through them. Címíng... [summarized]... [took charge of him].

Regarding the affairs of the monastery: although he had relied upon him for a long time, no realization had yet dawned. Whenever he sought instruction, Yuanmiao would say, "The affairs of the storehouse are busy; go now.

Later, monastics and laypeople welcomed him to reside at Yangqi, where his Dharma teachings flourished greatly. He subsequently moved to Yungai and passed away in the first year of the Huangyou era.

His stupa was erected at his original mountain. There were four disciples who inherited his Dharma: "A three-legged donkey trots along, Leaping and bounding, step by step, in accord with non-arising. Yangqi knows you have still not realized it— The elder of Hunan has his two eyebrows arched."

Linji’s lineage passed through seven transmissions to reach Shishuang Quan. Quan had two sons: one was Jicui Nan, and the other was Yangqi Hui. Nan’s pedagogical methods were like sitting at a crossroads where all manner of rare and wondrous goods are gathered for sale;

those who seek them may find whatever they require, whether it be a lost hairpin or a fallen earring. Consequently, among his later descendants, some could not avoid being spurious or overreaching. Hui, however, was like a jade carver refining a *fan-yu* gem; thus his descendants were all radiant and illuminating, truly upholding the family tradition—just as the *Biluo Stele* has no counterfeit versions.

The thirteenth patriarch, Chan Master Shouzhen Baoyun of Shuzhou, was a successor of Yangqi. He was the son of the Ge family of Hengyang. In his youth, he devoted himself to calligraphy and literature;

The Master replied, "Venerable Master Yuru of Chaling. Yangqi said, "I have heard that he once suffered a fall while crossing a bridge."

"I have attained some realization," [Zhaozhou] said. "The verse you composed is truly extraordinary; can you recite it? The Master recited it: "I possess a bright pearl, Long confined by the dust of worldly toil.
Today the dust is cleared and its light shines forth, Illuminating ten thousand peaks of mountains and rivers.

Yunqi smiled and hurried away. The Master was struck with astonishment and could not sleep all night. At dawn, he went to inquire after him. It happened to be the end of the year. Yunqi said, "Did you see..."
The Master asked, "Did you see those who performed the *dagu* exorcism yesterday? He replied, "I saw them. Qiji said, "In one respect, you are not his equal.
The Master was even more greatly startled and asked, "What do you mean by this? Qiji said, "He enjoys being laughed at; you fear being laughed at.

The Master attained great enlightenment and served as his attendant for a long time before taking leave to travel to Mount Lu. Later, Chan Master Netu of Yuan Tong was recommended to take up residence at Chengtian Temple, where his reputation became exceedingly prominent. Subsequently—
He moved to Fahua, Longmen, Xinghua, and Haihui; wherever he went, the assembly gathered like clouds (The cuckoo cries by the banks of the Wuling Stream;

"Responding to conditions and meeting with sentient beings without anything left unattended, yet always remaining upon this seat of Bodhi.
Great assembly, how would you explain the principle of responding to conditions and meeting with sentient beings?

In the mere snap of a finger, the capacities and karmic roots of all living beings throughout the entire world are simultaneously met and fully satisfied, yet not a single hair’s breadth has ever been moved. This, for now, is called 'responding.'"
Responding to conditions and karmic resonance, one constantly dwells upon this seat. It is just as when this mountain monk accepted the invitation for the *Lotus Sūtra* assembly;
I took my leave of the great assembly in succession, went to open the hall within Susong County, and only then returned to the monastery.
Now tell me: have I left this seat or not? If you say I have left, that is merely following worldly conventions. If you say I have not left, how can it be so?
"You have seen that which is inseparable. Is it not that the realms of boundless lands are not separated from one another by so much as a hair’s tip?
That the ten ages of past and present, from beginning to end, do not depart from this very moment of thought?
Or is it that all things, being without mind, are spontaneously pervasive at once? If you think so, you are merely striking at the moon with a falling staff. At this point, you must awaken."

After awakening, one must further encounter a person before realization is truly attained. If, having awakened, you encounter such a person at the time they extend their hand in skillful means, then at every step there will naturally be a path for you to emerge.

If you merely grasp the "dry radish-head" [superficial understanding], not only will you blind the eyes of future students, but you yourself will, upon every movement, first strike against the sharp edge and wound your own hands. You, the assembly, must know this: after awakening, one must encounter...
A person meets others at a crossroads, yet shakes hands atop a thousand peaks;
they meet atop a thousand peaks, yet shakes hands at a crossroads. Therefore, I, this mountain monk, have often composed a verse:
"Where others dwell, I do not dwell; where others travel, I do not travel. It is not that I find it difficult to act for others' sake."
Gathering together, one must generally distinguish clearly between the monastic and the lay. This matter is like letting go of one's hand atop a ten-thousand-fathom cliff:

one tumbles straight to the bottom, yet it is simply that one cannot relinquish one’s life-force. He passed away in the fifth year of the Xining era. Six people inherited his Dharma (Baoyun Baozhu was struck by Yangqi’s single laugh;

The Fourteenth Patriarch, Chan Master Fayan of Wuzhuo in Qizhou, was a successor of Baiyun.

A native of the Deng family from Mianzhou, at the age of thirty-five, he first left the household life to receive the tonsure and full ordination. He went to Chengdu to study treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Śataśāstra*.

There, he heard that when a Bodhisattva enters the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), wisdom merges with principle and the objective realm unites with the spirit, such that subject and object are no longer distinguished.

Regarding the realization of that which is realized, a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) challenged him, saying: "If there is no distinction between the subject that realizes and the object that is realized, then by what means is there realization?
No one could respond. The Master went to them and rescued this meaning, saying: "It is like a person drinking water; whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves.
This resolved the challenge. The Master then said: "The coldness and warmth may indeed be known, but what is the matter of the knowing itself? Thereupon, he went to question his own teacher.
The lecturer said, "To clarify this, you should go to the south and seek out one who has transmitted the school of the Buddha-mind.
The Master immediately took up his book-basket and crossed the pass. Whichever venerable elders he encountered, he consulted them all regarding this matter, yet his doubts remained unresolved.
He then went to visit Chan Master Fushan Yuan to request further instruction on the previous dialogue. Fushan said, "I have a metaphor that I will explain to you."

He received the tonsure at Shion-in at the age of twenty-four. While contemplating a flowing spring, he attained a realization;
he went to Mount Hōon to seek certification, but Hōun drove him away with blows. At that time, a rumor spread among the common people that the government was selecting young boys and girls.
The Master therefore asked Hōun, "If someone were to come and ask you, Preceptor, for a young boy or girl, what would you do? Hōun replied, "I simply hand over my bamboo staff."
He gave it to another. Under the Master’s words, he was without obstruction. Thereupon, Gaofeng wrote a true eulogy and presented it to the Master, saying:
"My appearance is inconceivable; even Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot behold it. I alone permit this unworthy child to have seen half of my nose.

He further instructed his disciples to go to the Master to seek further instruction. Consequently, students flocked to him like spokes converging on a hub, gathering as water flows downward. And so, the Master—
He continued to remain humble and concealed, never once being willing to assume the role of a teacher.

Whenever the prime ministers, high officials, and even the Emperor above, would leave the great monasteries of Jing Mountain and Lingyin vacant and present ceremonial gifts to welcome him, he ultimately could not be brought there.
At times, he would flee by crossing mountains or sailing across the sea; thus, he had no fixed residence. Nevertheless, every place he passed through became a sacred treasure.

In the neighborhood, both monastics and laypeople, men and women alike, regardless of their social rank, would bow down upon seeing the dust raised by his approach. Offerings of gold and silk were all received with equal regard.
When the Master first attended Gaofeng at the Deadman’s Barrier, he engaged in manual labor by day and practiced silent meditation by night.

He applied himself with such rigorous austerity that his ribs did not touch his mat for ten years. Through persistent inquiry and exhaustive investigation, he finally received the seal of transmission. After Gaofeng passed away...
Later, the Master resided either on a boat or in a hermitage, dwelling beside them as if they were illusory abodes.

Furthermore, when the imperial court heard of the Master’s spiritual influence, it conferred upon him the title "Chan Master Foci Yuanzhao Guanghui. At that time, there were no kings, dukes, or princes by marriage who did not pay him their respects;

Zhao Mengfu, the Grand Secretary of the Hanlin Academy, treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher and frequently inquired about the essentials of the Dharma. In his later years, he dwelt at Mount Tianmu. The year was Guihai.

In the eighth month, he manifested illness. To those who came to visit him, he said, "The Huanzhu Hermitage leaks from above and is drafty on the sides; the fences have collapsed and the walls have fallen.

It cannot be inhabited for long. He spoke and laughed as he did in his usual manner. When others urged him to take medicine, he said, "Under the blue sky and bright sun, would I bend my will to accommodate human sentiments?
He brushed them away. On the thirteenth day, he wrote a verse by hand to bid farewell to his lay patrons and fellow practitioners.
He was a member of the old [Linji] lineage. On the fourteenth day, he took his leave of the assembly early, saying: "I have one phrase to entrust to you all.

If you ask what it is, there is no fundamental basis upon which to rely. He set aside his writing brush, sat upright, and passed away. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Wangjiang Stone. There were four disciples who inherited the Dharma:

His mouth was like a surging wave, tossing and turning the great ocean; his mind was like the bright moon, illuminating past and present. He was accustomed to wielding the staff with eyes for those who had them, and was skilled at playing the stringless lute. As for this half-nose, who knows which person it belongs to?
[This is the record of his] knowledge.
The twenty-fourth [patriarch], Chan Master Qianyan Yuanchang of Shengshou Temple, known as the "Dragon Subdued by the World," was a successor of Zhongfeng.

He was a native of Xiaoshan County. His secular surname was Dong; his family lineage had long revered Confucianism. His father was Jiuding, and his mother was of the He clan. He was born late in life.

The Master wished to abandon him. His paternal aunt, Lady Xie, hurried to rescue him and raised him as her own son. At the age of seven, he entered the school of external teachers; whenever a book came before his eyes, he could recite it from memory.

His deportment was dignified whether entering or leaving, appearing as if he were already an adult. His father said with joy, "This son shall surely excel our clan through his literary talent and conduct.
There was a monk named Tanfang, who was of the Master’s paternal uncle's generation; he wished to request the Master to become his [disciple].
His successor, Lady Xie, challenged this view. Before long, the Master fell gravely ill. Lady Xie prayed to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and shortly thereafter he recovered.
She then followed him in his travels. At the age of seventeen, she scrutinized the teachings of the nine schools and the hundred masters;
subsequently, she abandoned them. At nineteen, she shaved her head and received full ordination, studying the Vinaya at Lingzhi Temple in Wulin during the reign of Emperor Xiaozong.
At a vegetarian feast hosted by the Chancellor’s office, the Master joined the assembly to receive offerings. At that time, Chan Master Zhongfeng Ben was already seated among them;
seeing the Master from afar, he called out, "How do you spend your daily life? The Master replied, "I recite the Buddha's name. Zhongfeng asked, "Where is the Buddha now?"
The Master hesitated to respond. Feng rebuked him with a stern voice. The Master knelt on his right knee and sought the essential points of the Dharma;
Feng bestowed upon him the "Mu" (No) koan of Zhaozhou and instructed him to investigate it. Thereupon, he bound himself with straw mats in the mountains of Lingyin. Suddenly, ten years passed.

He sighed, saying, "Throughout my life, my ambitions and spirit have filled the heavens and earth; how is it that I have now become a vinegar-gnat in a jar? Again, he sat so still that his ribs did not touch his mat.
He had been practicing the three-year mourning rite for his master. While traveling to Wangting, he heard the cry of a magpie and attained a realization.

He hurried to see Zhongfeng, who again rebuked him. The Master returned home in indignation. As the night drew toward stillness, a mouse suddenly ate the cat’s food; it fell into its bowl, making a sound.
Suddenly he attained awakening. He put on his robes and waited for dawn, then went again to consult Zhongfeng. Zhongfeng asked, "For what reason did Zhaozhou say 'no'?
The Master replied, "The rat ate the cat's food. Zhongfeng said, "Not yet. The Master said, "The vessel of rice has been broken. Zhongfeng asked, "What is it like after it is broken?
The Master said, "It is smashed against the square bricks. Zhongfeng then smiled and blessed the Master, saying, "You should take good care of yourself."

He protected and maintained [the Dharma], dwelling in seclusion within mountain caves. When the time arrived, the principle manifested of itself. Having received the entrustment, the Master retired to the Eastern Hermitage of Tianlong.

Later, his reputation and brilliance grew daily more prominent. Master Xing, the Chancellor of Zhongzhu, and Tuo-huan invited the Master to emerge from seclusion and assume the leadership of a monastery.
Accompanied by his disciple Xi-sheng, the Master traveled with his staff to Mount Fulong and took refuge beneath a great tree.
He resided there. The Emperor bestowed upon him the title "Buddha-Wisdom Perfect Mirror" (Fohui Yuanjian) and granted him a golden-embroidered Dharma robe.

In the sixth month of the Dingyou year of the Zhizheng era, he manifested illness. He wrote a verse, saying: "A lifetime of loquaciousness has now reached its end; one phrase roars through heaven, and the Eye of the True Dharma is extinguished.

Having set down his brush, he passed away. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at青松庵 (Qingsong Monastery). There were four successors to his Dharma lineage. (From the previous state of sleeping, he suddenly awoke.)
In recent years, the old koan has fallen into disuse: "Does the Buddha-nature exist or not? asks the old man Zhaozhou. (The blue sky and bright sun have no cause for coming or going.
The twenty-fifth patriarch was Chan Master Wanfeng Shiwei of Sheng'en Temple on Mount Deyun in Suzhou Prefecture;

he was the dharma heir of Qianyan. He was the son of the Jin family of Jinyue, Wenzhou, and his mother was Zheng. She dreamed that two figures, one a Confucian and the other a Buddhist, entered her bedchamber; upon waking, she [conceived him].

She gave birth to two sons; the Master was the youngest. Just as he was born, a light illuminated the room. Zheng was terrified and wished not to raise him, but his paternal aunt took charge of him and nurtured him.
While still in his swaddling clothes, whenever he saw a monk, he would immediately smile and make the gesture of joining his palms. His parents realized that he could not be kept [at home].
He caused the monk Sheng, the lecture master of Yongqing Temple in Yue, to leave the household life at the age of eleven.
He went to Hangzhou to receive full ordination and visited Chan Master Zhiyan at Hupao. Yan instructed him with the words of Nanquan regarding the "Three Is Not.
Consequently, he entered Mount Dapeng and established a hermitage at the ancient site of Foji Temple. Day and night he investigated his practice until he forgot both sleep and food. One.
One day, while listening to the Abbot of Wenxi Temple, Master Zongluei, recount the story of Guishan kicking over the water pitcher, [Wenxi] suddenly attained awakening.
He spoke a verse, saying: "Guishan’s ‘madness’ and ‘perversity’ are Nanquan; They have caused my diligent practice to be delayed for half a year.

If one could personally realize this right now, Why would he not strike with a fist straight to the chest? Thereupon, he went to see Zhuyan. However, by the time he arrived, Zhuyan had already passed away. The Master...

As soon as he entered the gate, Yanguan asked, "What do you bring to meet this old monk? The Master raised his fist and said, "I meet the Abbot here.

The Master replied, "The bubble arises and the bubble perishes, yet the water remains; the wind ceases and the waves subside, and the moon reflects in the pool. Yanguan then appointed him to the position of First Seat.
One day, Yanguan asked, "That which is not mind, not Buddha, and not a thing—what is it?
The Master drew a circle with his sitting cloth, stood with his hands clasped, and further presented this verse: "Nanquan was not trying to vex people's minds."
There was one who sought to take his mind to seize the mind, saying, "This is neither my mind nor the Buddha; the nature of heaven is vast and empty—what is there to seek?
Yanjun approved of this. Shortly thereafter, he withdrew once more into seclusion. When Master Qianyan invited him, he did not go, but instead sent his dharma robe and top-knot (ushnisha) to him.
Later, he planted his staff at Mount Dengwu in Suzhou, where practitioners flocked to him until it became a monastic community.

The twenty-sixth patriarch, Chan Master Baozang Puchi, was the second-generation successor who resided at Sheng’en.

The twenty-seventh patriarch, Chan Master Dongming Xubai Huida, was the successor of Baozang.
At the age of fourteen, he received the tonsure and precepts from Master Zhanran at Miaojue Temple in Danyang and went to Songyin in Yunjian to inquire about the seal of the mind.
However, [Songyin] did not yet grant his approval. He vowed that he would not cease until he attained thorough realization; consequently, he practiced meditative concentration for six days.

Emerging from meditation, he raised his head and beheld the pines; suddenly, he attained a profound realization. He then proceeded to Xuanmu Shengen Temple at the foot of the pines, where he met Master Guolin.
Their minds met like a needle and its eye fitting together. Guolin further directed him to see Chan Master Baozangchi, and he recounted the circumstances of his awakening.
Baozang rebuked him, saying, "The Buddha-dharma is like a vast ocean; the deeper one enters, the deeper it becomes. How can you rest content here?"
The Master then personally attended at the feet of the Venerable [Xuefeng]. One day, Zang asked him, "Mind is not Buddha; wisdom is not the Way. How do you understand this?

The Master stepped forward, inquired further, and stood with his hands joined in *añjali*. Zang rebuked him, saying, "Having been here for all this time, is this the kind of understanding you still possess?
The Master was then filled with indignation and forgot both sleep and food. By the second night, suddenly—
Having thoroughly penetrated the source and bottom of the Dharma, he then presented this verse: "A single punch shatters the great void;

Cangxiao said, "Even so, you must still protect and maintain yourself well. When the time arrives, the principle will manifest of itself. He then transmitted the Dharma to him.

The person (shatters the void, living with vivid clarity; the whole body surges forth, beyond all assumption. Vastly manifest, alone revealed, there is no private intent; in heaven or on earth, there is nowhere to hide).

The twenty-eighth patriarch, Chan Master Haizhou Puci of Dongming in Huzhou, was a native of Changshu in Suzhou. His surname was Qian, and his family had followed the Confucian profession for generations.
He left the household life at Poshan Temple and later went to Huiji Temple, where he listened to lectures on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

Upon reaching the passage that states, "Where there are only words and phrases, there is no real meaning," he remarked, "Today my words and phrases have only increased all the more. Thereupon, he returned home.
Day and night he read the sutras and investigated their true meaning, until his countenance grew increasingly haggard. A layman asked him, "Master, your complexion looks ill.
The Master replied, "It is because I have not yet clarified the Buddha-dharma; it is not illness.

The layman said, "If you have not clarified the Buddha-dharma, why do you not go to Mount Dengwu in the capital and seek instruction from Master Wanfeng? Upon hearing this, the Master was delighted and immediately—
He went to Dengwu and met Wanfeng. Wanfeng asked, "Where have you come from, śrāmaṇera? The Master prostrated, then rose and said, "From Changshu.
Wanfeng asked, "What brings you here? The Master recounted the previous conversation and bowed again, requesting instruction. Wanfeng then struck him twice across the head with his staff.
He stepped on Lanbei’s back and, kicking him twice with his feet, said, "This very thing is the true meaning. Lanbei had an awakening; he rose and said, "Excellent, excellent!

"The hair of a tortoise is entrusted to sons and grandsons; The horns of a hare are brought forth to seek the ford. A single shout leaves one deaf for three days; Within this, [the truth] is found."
"To whom can this news be entrusted? He further said, "You should conceal your traces and protect the Dharma; do not lightly act as a teacher or model for others.
The Master then built a hermitage in a valley of Mount Dongting and remained there for twenty-nine years.
One day, a monk arrived and asked, "What did you see on that day that led you to hide here and no longer go to visit other teachers? The Master replied, "In the past, I asked..."
Wanfeng said, "All verbal expressions are devoid of real meaning. Feng then struck him. From this, he attained enlightenment.
The monk asked, "Please tell me the reason why you attained it. The Master said, "One must simply know pain and itch; that is the real meaning, that is the wondrous mind.
All verbal expressions belong merely to the skin and hair. The monk said, "If one relies on such a view, one has not yet resolved the matter of birth and death. Why?"
He attained verbal proficiency but did not yet see the Way. He wondered, "Is it that the mind is not the Buddha, or that wisdom is not the Way?

By chance, the cord of an incense lamp snapped and fell to the ground; at that moment, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He went before the abbot to present his realization.
Ming said, "Old *jueluo*, you shall inherit the lineage of Wanfeng. The Master replied, "Master Bai brought me to full penetration; how could I inherit the lineage of Wanfeng?"
Dongming laughed. He then gathered the assembly, stepped out of the gate, and ascended the seat, saying: "Gautama had an intention for whom to transmit; Kāśyapa, without cause, broke into a smile.

"The lineage of the Ji school continues in an unbroken thread. Thereupon, he cast down his staff and descended from the seat. The Master immediately entered the abbot’s quarters to offer thanks.

The Master picked up the incense, pointed at Zhen, and said, "I nearly drowned you in a jar; fortunately it was Puci. Had it been anyone else, they could not have been saved.

A single incense offering to the Elder Dongming. With a heart of singular sincerity, he spurred me on, enabling me to penetrate the source of the lineage.
He gave two successive shouts; where one receives such deep grace, that is home. Only when one has milk does one know who one's mother is.
Rising from prostration, he wept bitterly and returned to the abbot’s quarters. On the eve of his passing, he spoke this verse: "Ninety-six years in this world, seventy..."
He served as a monk for forty years. Throughout this period, there were many points of ambiguity and contradiction. Upon seeing Dongming perish, he struck a circle with his whisk and said:
"From Śākyamuni to me, there have been sixty-two generations of countless old monks. He struck another circle and said: "Most have taken refuge here.

The twenty-ninth patriarch, Chan Master Baofeng Mingxuan, was a successor of Haizhou. He was a native of Wujiang in Gusu, surnamed Fan. In his lay life, he was a carpenter.
While working on the construction of a pagoda temple for Master Haizhou, his foot was struck by an axe.
In great pain, he asked for wine to drink. Upon hearing this, Haizhou went to him and said, "It is still bearable that you, Master Carpenter Fan, have injured your foot. However, if..."

"If I were to cut off your head, I would give you a thousand *shí* of wine to drink with it as your new head. Would you be able to drink it? The Master attained realization and immediately ceased drinking. He then requested to become a monk. Zhizhou immediately granted him the tonsure and said, "Today your head has fallen to the ground. The thirtieth patriarch, Chan Master Tianqi Bensui, was a successor of Baofeng. He was the son of the Jiang family of Zhongling in Nanchang.

At the age of twenty, while traveling with his father for trade in Yingzhou, he happened to grow weary of worldly phenomena. He then proceeded on foot to Jingmen, where he paid respects to Master Wushuo Neng and received the tonsure to become a śramaṇa.
He was instructed to contemplate the koan: "All dharmas return to One; to what does the One return?"

The Master then traveled extensively to consult senior masters and sat in meditation day and night. Upon reaching Guanyin Temple in Suizhou, he heard that Elder Jin was spending the summer retreat there.

The thirty-third generation successor, Chan Master Hanyou Zhengchuan Xiyuan of Jingxi, was born into the Lü clan of Liyang.
At the age of nineteen, he received the tonsure under Master Lè’ān. Because he suffered from a chronic illness, Lè’ān instructed him to contemplate the koan:
"Before the parents were yet born. After a long time, he achieved no realization; consequently, he applied himself with diligent perseverance for two periods of fourteen days.

A few days later, while walking in meditation one night, he was about to sit down when he was overcome by drowsiness. Unable to do anything about it, he suddenly heard the *bì-bào* (crackling) sound of a glass lamp’s wick burning out.
At that moment, he attained sudden enlightenment and said: "I now understand what the ancients meant when they said: 'The void is utterly pulverized; the great earth sinks into stillness;
in the ten directions there are no walls, and on the four sides there are no gates. If there were even one person who set forth the truth and returned to it..."
The teachings that "the empty space of the ten directions shall all vanish and perish," and so forth, are not false words.
